This pericope covers the departure of Jesus and His disciples across the brook Cedron into the garden of Gethsemane; the arrival of Judas with the cohort of soldiers and temple officers bearing lanterns, torches, and weapons; Christ's majestic self-revelation ("I am He") causing them to draw back and fall to the ground; Peter striking the high priest's servant Malchus; Christ's arrest and binding; His being led first to Annas; Peter's first denial outside the high priest's court; the interrogation of Jesus concerning His disciples and doctrine; the officer striking Jesus with the palm of his hand; and Christ being sent bound unto Caiaphas the high priest.

[^188]: Sessional Hymn in Tone 7 chanted after Antiphon 6 and the Second Passion Gospel (*Кі́й тѧ̀ ѻ҆́бразъ І҆ꙋ́до, преда́телѧ Сп҃сꙋ содѣ́ла* / *Ποῖός σε τρόπος Ἰούδα, προδότην τοῦ Σωτῆρος εἰργάσατο*). A celebrated patristic and hymnographic interrogation of Judas's motives, contrasting the singular privileges granted to him as an Apostle—sharing in the Apostolic choir, the charismatic gift of performing healings, reclining at the Mystical Supper, and having his feet washed by the Creator—with his base ingratitude and avarice. The hymn concludes by magnifying Christ's boundless long-suffering and great mercy.

[^189]: The Third Passion Gospel: Matthew 26:57–75 (section 109). Christ is brought before Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and elders are assembled; false witnesses seek testimony against Him; Caiaphas adjures Him by the living God to declare whether He is the Christ, the Son of God; Jesus confesses His divine identity and session at the right hand of Power; the high priest rends his clothes and condemns Him for blasphemy; the council spits in His face, buffets Him, and strikes Him with the palms of their hands; simultaneously, Peter sits in the courtyard, where he is recognized three times and denies the Lord with an oath; the cock crows, Peter remembers the word of the Lord, and he goes out weeping bitterly.

[^190]: Sessional Hymn in Tone 8 chanted after Antiphon 9 and the Third Passion Gospel (*Ѽ ка́кѡ І҆ꙋ́да и҆ногда̀ тво́й ᲂу҆чн҃къ* / *Ὦ πῶς Ἰούδας ποτὲ σοῦ ὁ μαθητής*). The hymn contrasts Judas's former fellowship as an Apostle with his treacherous bargain with the chief priests, whom he approached with hypocritical zeal, claiming to deliver Him Who "hath broken the Law and defiled the Sabbath."

[^191]: The Fourth Passion Gospel: John 18:28–19:16 (section 54). Christ is led early from Caiaphas unto the Roman praetorium before Pontius Pilate; the Jews refuse to enter the praetorium lest they be defiled; Pilate interrogates Jesus within concerning His kingship; Christ delivers His classic declaration that His Kingdom is not of this world, and that He came into the world to bear witness unto the truth; Pilate utters his cynical question "What is truth?" and attempts to release Jesus according to the Passover custom; the crowd demands Barabbas the robber; Pilate scourges Jesus and the soldiers crown Him with thorns, clothe Him in a purple robe, and strike Him; Pilate presents Him to the multitude with the immortal words "Behold the Man!" (*Ἴδε ὁ ἄνθρωπος* / *Сѐ Человѣ́къ*); the chief priests cry "Crucify Him!"; Pilate washes his hands of His blood; and upon the chief priests' declaration "We have no king but Caesar," Pilate delivers Him over to be crucified.

[^192]: Greek recensional variant troparion in Antiphon 10 (*Оу҆мирѝ мі́ръ, ѿ Дв҃ы и҆зво́ливый Гдⷭ҇и* / *Εἰρήνευσον τὸν κόσμον, ὁ ἐκ Παρθένου ἑλόμενος Κύριε*). In the 1907 Lviv Stauropegion edition, this troparion is printed with the explicit editorial rubrical heading `[ѿ Гре́ческагѡ.]` ("From the Greek") enclosed in brackets. This witnesses to the historical scholarly and recensional collation performed by the Stauropegion editors, incorporating Greek Triodion hymnographic witnesses into the Church Slavonic textus receptus.

[^193]: Sessional Hymn in Tone 8 chanted after Antiphon 12 and the Fourth Passion Gospel (*Е҆гда̀ предста́лъ є҆сѝ Каїа́фѣ Бж҃е* / *Ἡνίκα τῷ Καϊάφᾳ παρίστασο ὁ Θεός*). The hymn depicts the cosmic dread of the heavenly powers at the sight of the Supreme Judge standing before earthly tribunals (Caiaphas and Pilate), and His willing ascent upon the Cross between two thieves, numbered among the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12) to save fallen mankind.

[^194]: The Fifth Passion Gospel: Matthew 27:3–32 (section 111). Judas repents, confesses that he has betrayed innocent blood, casts down the thirty pieces of silver in the temple, and goes and hangs himself; the chief priests purchase the potter's field with the blood-money, fulfilling the prophecy of Zechariah/Jeremiah (Matthew 27:9–10); Jesus stands before Pilate the governor and remains silent; Pilate's wife sends word of her dream warning him to have nothing to do with that just man; the multitude chooses Barabbas and cries "Let Him be crucified!"; the Roman soldiers mock Christ in the praetorium, stripping Him, arraying Him in a scarlet robe, plaiting a crown of thorns upon His head, and placing a reed in His right hand; and leading Him away to Golgotha, they compel Simon of Cyrene to bear His cross.

[^195]: The Fifteenth Antiphon of Great Friday Matins, Tone 6 (*Дне́сь ви́ситъ на дре́вѣ* / *Σήμερον κρεμᾶται ἐπὶ ξύλου*). This hymn is universally recognized as the poetic and theological masterpiece of Great Friday hymnography. Composed in a sequence of six majestic parallel antitheses contrasting Christ's divine sovereignty with His kenotic humiliation: (1) He Who suspended the earth upon the waters hangs upon the Tree; (2) the King of angels is crowned with thorns; (3) He Who wraps the heavens in clouds is wrapped in a mock purple robe; (4) He Who freed Adam in the Jordan receives blows upon the face; (5) the Bridegroom of the Church is transfixed with nails; and (6) the Son of the Virgin is pierced with a lance. The antiphon concludes with the celebrated triple prostration: "We worship Thy Sufferings, O Christ! / We worship Thy Sufferings, O Christ! / We worship Thy Sufferings, O Christ! / Show us also Thy glorious Resurrection!"

[^196]: The Sessional Hymn (Kathisma / Troparion) in Tone 4 chanted after the 15th Antiphon and prior to the Sixth Passion Gospel (*И҆скꙋпи́лъ ны̀ є҆сѝ ѿ кла́твы зако́нныѧ* / *Ἐξηγόρασας ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου*). Based directly upon Galatians 3:13 ("Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangs on a tree"), this troparion summarizes the soteriological doctrine of the Atonement: by Christ's voluntary Crucifixion, piercing with the lance, and shedding of His precious Blood upon Golgotha, mankind is delivered from the condemnation of the Mosaic Law and endowed with divine immortality.

[^197]: The Sixth Passion Gospel: Mark 15:16–32 (section 67). This pericope recounts the mocking of Christ by the Roman cohort in the praetorium, where they clothe Him in purple, crown Him with thorns, strike Him upon the head with a reed, spit upon Him, and bow their knees before Him in derision; His procession to Golgotha, with Simon of Cyrene compelled to bear His cross; His refusal of the wine mingled with myrrh; His crucifixion at the third hour; the division of His garments by casting lots; the superscription of His accusation ("The King of the Jews"); His crucifixion between two thieves; the mockery of the passers-by, chief priests, and scribes ("He saved others; Himself He cannot save... Let Christ the King of Israel descend now from the cross, that we may see and believe"); and the reviling of the thieves crucified with Him.

[^198]: Psalm 21:19 (LXX 21:18): *Раздѣли́ша ри̑зы моѧ̑ себѣ̀, и҆ ѡ҆ ѻ҆де́жди мое́й мета́ша жре́бїй* ("They parted My garments among them, and upon My vesture they cast lots"). In the liturgical structure of Passion Matins, this prokeimenon in Tone 4 introduces the Seventh Passion Gospel, highlighting the direct fulfillment of Davidic messianic prophecy in the crucifixion narrative.

[^199]: The Seventh Passion Gospel: Matthew 27:33–54 (section 113). The arrival at Golgotha; offering of vinegar mingled with gall; the crucifixion and casting lots for His garments; the setting up of the accusation ("This is Jesus the King of the Jews"); the railing of the passers-by and elders; the darkness over all the land from the sixth unto the ninth hour; Christ's loud cry at the ninth hour: *"Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani"*; the offering of the sponge filled with vinegar on a reed; Christ crying again with a loud voice and yielding up the ghost; the tearing in twain of the temple veil from top to bottom; the earthquake and rending of rocks; the opening of the graves and resurrection of many bodies of the saints; and the confession of the centurion and those watching Jesus: *"Truly this was the Son of God."*

[^200]: Rubric for patristic reading: *(И҆ полага́етсѧ чте́нїе)* — "And a reading is appointed." Following the Seventh Passion Gospel and preceding Psalm 50, traditional liturgical typika (including the Evergetis, Studite, and Ruthenian Stauropegion traditions) appoint a solemn patristic homily on the Lord's Passion, typically selected from St. John Chrysostom, St. Ephrem the Syrian, or St. Cyril of Alexandria.

[^201]: The Eighth Passion Gospel: Luke 23:32–49 (section 114). The leading away of two evildoers to be put to death with Jesus at Calvary; Christ's prayer for His executioners: *"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do"*; the dividing of His garments; the derision of the rulers and soldiers offering vinegar; the superscription in letters of Greek, Latin, and Hebrew; the dialogue of the two thieves, wherein the repentant thief confesses Christ's innocence and cries: *"Lord, remember me when Thou comest into Thy kingdom"*, receiving the Lord's divine promise: *"Truly I say unto thee, Today shalt thou be with Me in paradise"*; the darkness over all the earth until the ninth hour; the sun darkened and veil rent; Christ's final commendation: *"Father, into Thy hands I commend My spirit"*; and the centurion glorifying God and declaring: *"Certainly this was a righteous man."*

[^202]: The Three-Ode Canon (Triodion / Tripesnets) of Great Friday Matins, composed by St. Cosmas the Melodist (Bishop of Maiuma, c. 675–752). Comprising Odes 5, 8, and 9 in Tone 6, the canon directly reflects Byzantine hymnographic structure for the Holy and Great Friday vigil. The rubric directs the heirmoi to be chanted twice and the troparia twelve times (interpolating the stichological refrains between the troparia), concluding with a joint katavasia by both choirs chanting the heirmos together.

[^203]: The acrostic (*краегране́сїе*) of St. Cosmas's Three-Ode Canon: *Проса́вватонъ те* (Greek: Προσάββατόν τε), signifying "And the eve of the Sabbath" (the day before the Sabbath, i.e., Friday). Across Odes 5, 8, and 9, the twelve troparia spell out this exact Greek acrostic in their original Byzantine verses, preserved here faithfully in Church Slavonic translation with the acrostic letters explicitly indicated in the margins: Ode 5 (`П`, `Р`, `О`), Ode 8 (`С`, `А`, `В`, `В`, `А`), and Ode 9 (`Т`, `О`, `Н`, `Т`, `Є`).

[^204]: The Kontakion of Holy and Great Friday in Tone 8 (*На́съ ра́ди Распѧ́таго, прїиди́те всѝ воспои́мъ* / *Τὸν δι' ἡμᾶς σταυρωθέντα, δεῦτε πάντες ὑμνήσωμεν*), composed by St. Romanos the Melodist (6th century). This kontakion introduces Romanos's celebrated poetic dialogue between the Virgin Mary and her Son on His way to Golgotha, emphasizing that Mary's confession of faith transcends the shame of the Cross: *"Though Thou dost endure crucifixion, Thou art my Son and my God!"*

[^205]: The Ikos of Holy and Great Friday (*Своего̀ А҆́гнца А҆́гница зрѧ́щи* / *Τὸν ἴδιον Ἄρνα θεωροῦσα ἡ Ἀμνάς*), forming the strophe of St. Romanos's kontakion. The Virgin Mary, seeing her Lamb led to slaughter, addresses Him with maternal pathos, asking whether He is hastening to another wedding in Cana of Galilee to turn water into wine, and begging the divine Logos not to pass her by in silence, but to speak a word of comfort to the Mother who bare Him.

[^206]: The Synaxarion of Holy and Great Friday, compiled by the 14th-century Byzantine ecclesiastical historian Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos. The opening distich verses on the Crucifixion (*Живы́й є҆сѝ Бж҃е ты̀, и҆ ᲂу҆мерщвле́нный на дре́вѣ* / *Ζωὸς πέφυκας, ὦ Θεός, νεκρὸς δὲ σύ· Ὦ νεκρὲ γυμνέ, καὶ Θεοῦ ζῶντος Λόγε*) and on the thief (*Заключе́ннаѧ ѿве́рзе Е҆де́мскаѧ врата̀* / *Κεκλεισμένας ἤνοιξε τῆς Ἐδὲμ πύλας, Βαλὼν ὁ λῃστὴς κλεῖδα, τὸ Μνήσθητί μου*) encapsulate the cosmic paradox of the Creator dying in the flesh and opening paradise through the repentant thief's prayer. The narrative prose recounts the full chronological progression of Christ's trials before Annas, Caiaphas, and Pilate, the release of Barabbas, the scourging and crowning with thorns, the crucifixion at Golgotha, the supernatural portents, the piercing of the side, and the burial by Joseph and Nicodemus.

[^207]: *Lithostrotos* (Greek: Λιθόστρωτον; Hebrew/Aramaic: Gabbatha, John 19:13): the elevated stone pavement where Pilate sat on the judgment seat. The Synaxarion connects this biblical site with the Jewish and early Christian theological tradition regarding Solomon covering Adam's skull with a mound of stones, whence the name of the place was derived.

[^208]: The patristic theological exposition of the Crucifixion in the Synaxarion: St. Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos expounds the typology of the Passion: Christ is crucified on Friday (the 6th day) and at the 6th hour because man was created on the 6th day and Adam stretched forth his hand to the tree at the 6th hour; the garden of the tomb corresponds to the Garden of Eden; the bitter drink heals the tasting of the forbidden fruit; the buffeting confers freedom; the spittings restore human honor; the crown of thorns removes the curse of the earth; the scarlet robe replaces the coats of skins; the nails arrest the movement of sin; the pierced side heals the wound of Adam's rib from which Eve was formed; the lance wards off the cherubim's flaming sword; the water from the side prefigures baptism; and the blood poured forth upon Adam's skull beneath Golgotha signifies the mystical baptism and redemption of fallen humanity by the New Adam.

[^209]: The Exapostilarion of Holy and Great Friday (*Разбо́йника бл҃горазꙋ́мнаго во є҆ди́номъ часѣ̀ ра́еви сподо́билъ є҆сѝ Гдⷭ҇и* / *Τὸν λῃστὴν αὐθημερὸν τοῦ παραδείσου ἠξίωσας, Κύριε*). Chanted thrice with great solemnity at the conclusion of the Three-Ode Canon, this hymn is one of the most beloved masterpieces of the Passion services, begging the Savior to enlighten the believer by the wood of the Cross even as He received the repentant thief into paradise.

[^210]: The Ninth Passion Gospel: John 19:25–37 (section 61). Standing by the Cross: His Mother, Mary the wife of Cleopas, and Mary Magdalene; Christ commending His Mother unto the beloved disciple John: *"Woman, behold thy son!"* and to the disciple: *"Behold thy mother!"*; Christ's cry: *"I thirst"*; the sponge filled with vinegar put upon hyssop and placed to His mouth; Christ's triumph: *"It is finished"*; bowing His head and giving up the ghost; the soldiers breaking the legs of the first and the other thief, but finding Jesus already dead, they broke not His legs, fulfilling Scripture (*"A bone of Him shall not be broken"*, Ex. 12:46, Ps. 33:21); one of the soldiers piercing His side with a lance, and forthwith blood and water coming out; and the testimony of the eyewitness disciple, fulfilling Zechariah 12:10 (*"They shall look on Him Whom they pierced"*).

[^211]: The Doxastikon (Glory) of the Praises (Lauds) in Tone 6 (*Совлеко́ша съ менѐ ри̑зы моѧ̑* / *Ἐξέδυσάν με τὰ ἱμάτιά μου*). A prophetic monologue of the suffering Messiah, drawing directly upon Psalm 2:9 (*"Thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel"*) and the gospel accounts of the Roman soldiers stripping Him, placing the scarlet robe upon Him, crowning Him with thorns, and placing the reed in His hand.

[^212]: The Theotokion / Sticheron (Both now) of the Praises in Tone 6 (*Плещи̑ моѧ̑ да́хъ на ра̑ны* / *Τὸν νῶτόν μου ἔδωκα εἰς μάστιγας*). Drawing directly upon the Third Servant Song of Isaiah (Isaiah 50:6: *"I gave My back to the smiters, and My cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not My face from shame and spitting"*), this hymn confesses Christ's voluntary endurance of the tribunal of Pilate and the cross for the salvation of the world.

[^213]: The Tenth Passion Gospel: Mark 15:43–47 (section 69). Joseph of Arimathea, an honorable counselor who waited for the Kingdom of God, goes boldly unto Pilate and cravs the body of Jesus; Pilate marvels if He were already dead, and calling the centurion, asks whether He had been any while dead; upon the centurion's confirmation, Pilate gives the body to Joseph; Joseph buys fine linen, takes Him down, wrapps Him in the linen, and lays Him in a sepulchre hewn out of a rock, rolling a stone unto the door; and Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses behold where He was laid.

[^214]: The Eleventh Passion Gospel: John 19:38–42 (section 62). Joseph of Arimathea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, beseeches Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus; Pilate grants permission; Nicodemus comes also, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight; they take the body of Jesus and wind it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury; in the place where He was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new sepulchre wherein was never man yet laid; there they lay Jesus because of the Jews' preparation day, for the sepulchre was nigh at hand.

[^215]: Psalm 68:22 (LXX 68:21): *Да́ша въ снѣ́дь мою̀ же́лчь, и҆ въ жа́ждꙋ мою̀ напои́ша мѧ̀ ѻ҆́цта* ("They gave Me gall for My food, and for My thirst they gave Me vinegar to drink"). A messianic stichos chanted before the third aposticha sticheron of Great Friday.

[^216]: Psalm 73:12 (LXX 73:12): *Бг҃ъ же Цр҃ь на́шъ, пре́жде вѣ́ка содѣ́ла спасе́нїе посредѣ̀ землѝ* ("But God is our King of old, He hath wrought salvation in the midst of the earth"). Appointed as the final stichos of the Aposticha, confessing the cosmic and eternal scope of the Redemption accomplished on Golgotha.

[^217]: The Twelfth Passion Gospel: Matthew 27:62–66 (section 114). The final Passion Gospel, chanted immediately after the Aposticha at the conclusion of Great Friday Matins. On the morrow after the preparation day, the chief priests and Pharisees gather before Pilate, recalling Christ's prophecy: *"After three days I will rise again"*; they request that the sepulchre be made secure until the third day, lest His disciples come by night, steal Him away, and say unto the people: *"He is risen from the dead"*; Pilate grants them a guard (*"Ye have a watch: go your way, make it as sure as ye can"*); and they go and make the sepulchre sure, sealing the stone and setting a watch.

[^218]: The Troparion of Holy and Great Friday in Tone 4 (*И҆скꙋпи́лъ ны̀ є҆сѝ ѿ кла́твы зако́нныѧ* / *Ἐξηγόρασας ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου*). Rooted in Galatians 3:13 ("Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us"), this hymn summarizes the entire theological drama of the Twelve Passion Gospels: by Christ's voluntary Crucifixion and piercing with the lance, the curse of the Law is dissolved and divine immortality is poured forth upon mankind.

[^219]: The solemn Great Friday Passion Dismissal: following the exclamation of the litany, the priest pronounces the special kenotic dismissal commemorating Christ's voluntary humiliation: *"May He Who endured spittings, and scourgings, and buffetings, the Cross and death, for our salvation, Christ our true God..."*

[^220]: The concluding Typikon rubric of Great Friday Matins: *(Пе́рвый же ча́съ не совокꙋплѧ́емъ ны́нѣ, но ѡ҆ второ́мъ часѣ̀ днѐ)* — "The First Hour we do not join now, but at the second hour of the day." In normal daily liturgical practice, the First Hour is attached directly to the end of Matins. On Holy and Great Friday, however, the First Hour is separated from Matins and chanted later in the morning (at the second hour, approximately 8:00 AM) together with the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Royal Hours (*Царскіе Часы*), which form a single extended monumental liturgical office with special psalms, prokeimena, Old Testament prophecies, Epistles, and Gospels.

[^221]: The Order of the Royal Hours of Holy and Great Friday (*Сказа́нїе часѡ́въ ст҃а́гѡ и҆ вели́кагѡ Пѧтка̀*), traditionally attributed in the liturgical title to St. Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria (c. 376–444). The service combines the First, Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours into an extended monumental office of the Passion, celebrated with the striking of the klepalo, the priest vesting in epitrachelion and phelonion, and the solemn chanting of special psalms, stichera idiomela, Old Testament prophecies, Epistles, and Gospels.

[^222]: Psalm 5 (LXX 5): *Глаго́лы моѧ̑ внꙋшѝ Гдⷭ҇и* ("Give ear to my words, O Lord"). Appointed as the opening psalm of the First Hour, emphasizing morning prayer and the righteous appeal to God against the assembly of deceitful, boastful, and bloodthirsty adversaries.

[^223]: Psalm 2 (LXX 2): *Вскꙋ́ю шата́шасѧ ꙗ҆зы́цы* ("Why have the heathen raged"). A foundational Davidic messianic psalm appointed for the First Royal Hour, prophesying the kings of the earth and the rulers taking counsel together against the Lord and against His Anointed (Christ), directly fulfilled in the Sanhedrin, Herod, and Pontius Pilate's tribunal.

[^224]: Psalm 21 (LXX 21): *Бж҃е, Бж҃е мо́й, вонми́ ми, вскꙋ́ю ѡ҆ста́вилъ мѧ̀ є҆сѝ* ("O God, my God, attend unto me; why hast Thou forsaken me?"). The preeminent prophetic psalm of the Passion, whose opening cry was uttered by Christ upon the Cross (Matt. 27:46, Mark 15:34), detailing the mockery of the bystanders, the piercing of His hands and feet, the dividing of His garments, and the casting of lots.

[^225]: Troparion of the First Hour in Tone 1: *Распе́ншꙋсѧ тебѣ̀ Хрⷭ҇тѐ, поги́бе мꙋчи́тельство* ("When Thou wast crucified, O Christ, the tyranny was destroyed"). Commemorating the voluntary Passion of the Savior which vanquished the hostile power of the devil without angelic or human intervention.

[^226]: Theotokion of the First Hour: *Что́ тѧ нарече́мъ, ѽ Ѽбра́дованнаѧ;* ("What shall we call thee, O thou full of grace?"). A classic Marian theological hymn celebrating the Mother of God under the typological titles of Heaven, Paradise, Virgin, and Pure Mother.

[^227]: The Stichera Idiomela of the First Hour: three stichera selected from the twelve solemn troparia of the Passion chanted across the Royal Hours. Chanted responsively between the two choirs with Psalm verses: Tone 8 (*Дне́сь церко́внаѧ завѣ́са*), Tone 8 (*Ꙗ҆́кѡ ѻ҆вча̀ на заколе́нїе*), and Tone 8 (*Є҆́мшымъ тѧ̀ беззако́ннымъ*).

[^228]: Old Testament Prophecy of the First Hour: Zechariah 11:10–14; 12:10; 13:7; 14:6–9, 20–21. A composite prophetic pericope containing Zechariah's remarkable messianic prophecies: the thirty pieces of silver cast into the furnace in the house of the Lord, the piercing of the Messiah ("they shall look upon Him Whom they have pierced"), the striking of the Shepherd and scattering of the sheep, and the cosmic darkening of the sun on that unique day known only to the Lord.

[^229]: Epistle of the First Hour: Galatians 6:14–18 (section 215 from the half). St. Paul's triumphant apostolic confession: *"God forbid that I should boast, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by Whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world."*

[^230]: Gospel of the First Hour: Matthew 27:1–56 (section 110). The monumental Passion narrative according to Matthew: the council of the chief priests and elders; Judas's remorse, return of the thirty pieces of silver, and death; the trial before Pontius Pilate; the release of Barabbas; the scourging and crowning with thorns; the journey to Golgotha with Simon of Cyrene; the Crucifixion between two thieves; the derision; the darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour; Christ's death; the tearing of the temple veil; the resurrection of many saints; and the confession of the centurion.

[^231]: Concluding Prayer of the First Hour: *Хрⷭ҇тѐ свѣ́те и҆́стинный* ("O Christ, the true Light, Who enlightenest and sanctifiest every man that comes into the world").

[^232]: Psalm 34 (LXX 34): *Сꙋдѝ Гдⷭ҇и, ѡ҆би́дѧщымъ мѧ̀* ("Judge them, O Lord, that wrong me"). The first appointed psalm of the Third Royal Hour, praying for divine vindication against false witnesses and unrighteous persecutors who reward evil for good.

[^233]: Psalm 108 (LXX 108): *Бж҃е, хвалы̀ моеѧ̀ не премолчѝ* ("O God of my praise, hold not Thy peace"). A severe imprecatory and prophetic psalm directly applied in the New Testament (Acts 1:20) to Judas the Iscariot and the deicidal persecutors of Christ: *"Let his days be few, and his bishopric let another take."*

[^234]: Psalm 50 (LXX 50): The universal penitential psalm of King David (*Поми́лꙋй мѧ̀ Бж҃е* / "Have mercy on me, O God"), chanted at the Third Hour to evoke profound contrition and inward cleansing before the mystery of the Cross.

[^235]: Troparion of the Third Hour in Tone 6: *Гдⷭ҇и, ѡ҆сꙋди́ша тѧ̀ І҆ꙋде́е на сме́рть* ("O Lord, the Jews condemned Thee unto death, Who art the Life of all"). Contrasting Israel's miraculous deliverance through the Red Sea and water from the rock with their handing over of Christ to death and offering Him gall and vinegar.

[^236]: The Stichera Idiomela of the Third Hour: Tone 8 (*Стра́ха ра́ди І҆ꙋде́йскагѡ*), Tone 8 (*Пре́жде чⷭ҇тна́гѡ твоегѡ̀ крⷭ҇та̀*), and Tone 5 (*Влекомь на крⷭ҇тъ си́це вопїѧ́лъ є҆сѝ Гдⷭ҇и*), recounting Peter's denial and repentance, the mocking by the Roman soldiers, and Christ's sorrowful reproaches to the Jewish people.

[^237]: Old Testament Prophecy of the Third Hour: Isaiah 50:4–11. The Third Servant Song of Isaiah: *"I gave My back to the smiters, and My cheeks to blows; I hid not My face from the shame of spitting."*

[^238]: Epistle of the Third Hour: Romans 5:6–10 (section 118 from the half). St. Paul's theological discourse on divine reconciliation: while we were yet sinners and enemies, Christ died for the ungodly, and we are justified by His Blood.

[^239]: Gospel of the Third Hour: Mark 15:16–41 (sections 67 and 68 in series). St. Mark's account of the Roman soldiers mocking Christ in the praetorium, Simon of Cyrene carrying the Cross, the Crucifixion at the third hour, the superscription, the mockery of the priests and scribes, the darkness at the sixth hour, Christ's death at the ninth hour, the tearing of the veil, and the centurion's confession.

[^240]: The Prayer of Saint Mardarios: *Влⷣко Бж҃е Ѻ҆́ч҃е Вседержи́телю* ("O Master God, Father Almighty, O Lord the Only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, and Holy Spirit: one Godhead, one Power, have mercy on me a sinner; and by the judgments which Thou knowest, save me Thine unworthy servant, for Thou art blessed unto ages of ages. Amen.").

[^241]: The Order of the Sixth Hour of Holy and Great Friday: opening with the royal psalms Psalm 53 (LXX 53, *Бж҃е, во и҆́мѧ твоѐ спаси́ мѧ*), Psalm 139 (LXX 139, *И҆зми́ мѧ Гдⷭ҇и, ѿ человѣ́ка лꙋка́ва*), and Psalm 90 (LXX 90, *Живы́й въ по́мощи Вы́шнѧгѡ*), focusing on the midday hour of the Crucifixion when Christ was nailed to the Cross between the two thieves.

[^242]: Troparion of the Sixth Hour, Tone 2: *Спасе́нїе содѣ́лалъ є҆сѝ посредѣ̀ землѝ Хрⷭ҇тѐ Бж҃е* ("Thou hast wrought salvation in the midst of the earth, O Christ God"). Commemorating Christ stretching out His most pure hands upon the Cross to gather all the nations into unity.

[^243]: Stichera Idiomela of the Sixth Hour: Tone 8 (*Сїѧ̑ глаго́летъ Гдⷭ҇ь І҆ꙋде́ѡмъ*), Tone 8 (*Законополо́жницы І҆и҃левы, І҆ꙋде́е и҆ фарісе́е*), and Tone 5 (*Прїиди́те Хрⷭ҇тоно́снїи лю́дїе*). The divine reproaches contrasting the wonders of the Exodus (manna, water from the rock) with the vinegar and gall, and Christ's prayer for His crucifiers: *"Father, forgive them this sin."*

[^244]: Old Testament Prophecy of the Sixth Hour: Isaiah 52:13–54:1. The Fourth Servant Song of Isaiah: the suffering, humiliation, and vicarious atonement of the Servant of the Lord (*"He was wounded for our sins, and tormented for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon Him, and by His stripe we are healed"*).

[^245]: Epistle of the Sixth Hour: Hebrews 2:11–18 (section 306). St. Paul's theological discourse on the Incarnation: Christ took part of flesh and blood that through death He might destroy the devil who had the power of death, becoming a merciful and faithful High Priest.

[^246]: Gospel of the Sixth Hour: Luke 23:32–49 (section 111). St. Luke's account of the Crucifixion between two malefactors, the prayer of Christ for His executioners, the salvation of the prudent thief (*"Today shalt thou be with Me in Paradise"*), the darkness over all the earth from the sixth to the ninth hour, and Christ's final commendation into the hands of the Father.

[^247]: Liturgical patristic reading after the Gospel of the Sixth Hour: customarily from the Catechetical Lectures of St. Cyril of Jerusalem (Catechesis 13) or St. John Chrysostom's Homily on the Cemetery and the Cross.

[^248]: The Prayer of the Sixth Hour by Saint Basil the Great: *Бж҃е и҆ Гдⷭ҇и си́лъ, и҆ всеѧ̀ тва́ри Содѣ́телю* ("O God and Lord of hosts, and Maker of all creation"), beseeching God to nail our flesh to His fear, wound our souls with His love, and guide us into His unapproachable and everlasting light.

[^249]: The Order of the Ninth Hour of Holy and Great Friday: marking the solemn hour of 3:00 PM when our Lord Jesus Christ, having tasted the vinegar and cried with a loud voice, gave up the ghost upon the Cross.

[^250]: Psalm 68 (LXX 68, *Спаси́ мѧ Бж҃е, ꙗ҆́кѡ внидо́ша во́ды до дꙋшѝ моеѧ̀*), the paramount Messianic Passion psalm, directly prophesying Christ's thirst, the gall and vinegar (*"They gave Me gall for My food, and in My thirst they gave Me vinegar to drink"*), and the reproaches of those that reviled God falling upon Him.

[^251]: Psalm 69 (LXX 69, *Бж҃е, въ по́мощь мою̀ вонмѝ*), David's urgent cry for divine aid against mockers and persecution, traditional to the opening of the Ninth Hour.

[^252]: Psalm 85 (LXX 85, *Приклонѝ Гдⷭ҇и ᲂу҆́хо твоѐ, и҆ ᲂу҆слы́ши мѧ̀*), a prayer of profound humility and trust in God's great mercy, foretelling the worship of all nations before the true God.

[^253]: Troparion of the Ninth Hour in Tone 8: *Ви́дѧ разбо́йникъ Нача́льника жи́зни на крⷭ҇тѣ̀ ви́сѧща* ("Seeing the Author of life hanging upon the Cross, the thief said..."), praising the faith of the thief who recognized the crucified Lord as God through the cosmic signs in creation.

[^254]: The Stichera Idiomela of the Ninth Hour: Tone 7 (*Оу҆́жасъ бѣ̀ ви́дѣти*), Tone 2 (*Є҆гда̀ на крⷭ҇тѣ̀ пригвозди́ша беззако́ннїи*), and Tone 6 (*Дне́сь ви́ситъ на Дре́вѣ* / "Today He Who hung the earth upon the waters is hung upon the Tree"). The 15th Antiphon of Great Friday Matins incorporated into the Royal Hours, culminating in the threefold veneration of the Passion and prayer for the Resurrection.

[^255]: Old Testament Prophecy of the Ninth Hour: Jeremiah 11:18–23; 12:1–5, 9–11, 14–15. Commemorating the Prophet Jeremiah as a type of the innocent Lamb led to the slaughter (*"I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter; and I knew not that they had devised devices against me"*).

[^256]: Physical Leaf p79 = Printed Folio 74 + 5. The printed text abbreviates the Ninth Hour reading of Jeremiah with the rubric: *"Look in Great Thursday at the 1st Hour, folio 74"* (*И҆щѝ въ Четверто́къ вели́кїй на а҃-мъ часѣ̀, ли́стъ ѻ҃д*).

[^257]: Epistle of the Ninth Hour: Hebrews 10:19–31 (section 324). St. Paul on entering the Holy of Holies through the veil of Christ's flesh by His Blood, warning against counting the Blood of the covenant an unholy thing or outraging the Spirit of grace.

[^258]: Gospel of the Ninth Hour: John 18:28–19:37 (sections 61 and 62). St. John's Passion Gospel: the trial before Pilate, the scourging and crowning with thorns, *Ecce Homo*, the Crucifixion at Golgotha, the commending of the Mother of God to the beloved disciple, Christ's death, the piercing of His side with a lance, and the witness of blood and water.

[^259]: Liturgical patristic reading after the Gospel of the Ninth Hour: *The Homily on the Cross* (*Сло́во крⷭ҇тное*), traditional to the Sabaite and Studite Royal Hours, drawn from St. John Chrysostom or St. Cyril of Alexandria.

[^260]: The Prayer of the Ninth Hour: *Влⷣко Гдⷭ҇и І҆и҃се Хрⷭ҇тѐ Бж҃е на́шъ, долготерпѣ́вый ѡ҆ на́шихъ согрѣше́нїихъ* ("O Master, Lord Jesus Christ our God, Who hast long-suffered over our transgressions"), commemorating Christ's opening of Paradise to the prudent thief and petitioning for the mortification of carnal mind and renewal of the inner man.

[^261]: The Typika (Beatitudes) chanted quickly at the end of the Royal Hours, followed by the heavenly choir hymn, the Creed, the Kontakion of Great Friday, Psalm 33, and the final dismissal.

[^262]: Sabaite Typikon rubric for Great and Holy Friday: total aliturgical day (neither Presanctified nor Divine Liturgy is permitted) and strict fast without common meal or cooked food. Citing the Apostolic Constitutions (Book V, ch. 18) and the Canonical Epistle of St. Dionysius the Great of Alexandria (canon 1, PG 10:1272–1277) on the duration of the Paschal fast.

[^263]: Full-page copperplate engraving facing Great Friday Vespers: The Crucifixion of Christ with the Most Holy Mother of God and the Holy Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian standing at the foot of the Cross upon Mount Golgotha, with the titulus *I.N Ц.I.*, the skull of Adam, and the caption: *"For God so loved the world..."* (John 3:16).

[^264]: The solemn Vespers of Holy and Great Friday, marking the descent from the Cross and the burial of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. In Ruthenian liturgical practice (both Kyivan and Lviv recensions), this service culminates in the solemn procession with the Plashchanytsia (Holy Shroud) to the mystical tomb (sepulchre) positioned in the center of the nave for veneration.

[^265]: Liturgical timekeeping: the tenth hour of the day corresponds to approximately 4:00 PM (16:00), marking the late afternoon when Joseph of Arimathea obtained permission from Pontius Pilate to take down the Body of the Lord from the Cross.

[^266]: Psalm 21:19 (LXX 21:18, *Раздѣли́ша ри̑зы моѧ̑ себѣ̀*), the prophetic Passion psalm cited directly in Matthew 27:35 and John 19:24. The verse (*Стї́хъ*) is Psalm 21:2 (LXX 21:1, *Бж҃е Бж҃е мо́й, вонми́ ми, вскꙋ́ю ѡ҆ста́вилъ мѧ̀ є҆сѝ*), Christ's fourth word from the Cross (*Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani*).

[^267]: The First Old Testament Reading of Great Friday Vespers: Exodus 33:11–23. Moses's intimate dialogue with God in the Tabernacle of Witness and the divine theophany on Mount Sinai. Moses desires to see God's glory, but God declares that no man can see His face and live; God hides Moses in a cleft of the rock and covers him with His hand, revealing His back parts as He passes by. Typologically interpreted by the Holy Fathers as prefiguring Christ's burial in the rock tomb and the mystery of the Incarnate Godhead revealed in His suffering humanity.

[^268]: Psalm 34:1–2 (LXX 34:1–2, *Сꙋдѝ Гдⷭ҇и ѡ҆би́дѧщымъ мѧ̀*), David's prayer for divine deliverance against unrighteous oppressors, typifying the innocent Christ before the Sanhedrin and Pilate.

[^269]: The Second Old Testament Reading of Great Friday Vespers: Job 42:12–17 with the Septuagint epilogue (*та́кѡ толкꙋ́етсѧ ѿ сѷ́рскїѧ кни́ги* / "thus is it interpreted from the Syriac book"). The restoration of Job after his deep suffering, the naming of his three daughters (Day, Cassia, and Amalthea's Horn), his longevity and vision of four generations, and the explicit prophecy of his resurrection with those whom the Lord raises up. The Septuagint genealogical appendix identifies Job with Jobab, the fifth generation from Abraham through Esau (Genesis 36:33).

[^270]: The Third Old Testament Reading of Great Friday Vespers: Isaiah 52:13–54:1. The Fourth Servant Song of Isaiah, prophesying Christ's vicarious suffering, silent endurance, and ultimate vindication.

[^271]: Physical Leaf p130 = Printed Folio 124 + 5. The printed text abbreviates the reading of Isaiah 52:13–54:1 with the internal cross-reference rubric: *"Look in the 6th Hour, folio 124"* (*И҆щѝ на ѕ҃-мъ часѣ̀, ли́стъ рк҃д*).

[^272]: Prokeimenon of the Apostle, Tone 6: Psalm 87:7, 2 (LXX 87:6, 1, *Положи́ша мѧ̀ въ ро́вѣ преисподнѣ́йшемъ*), the most desolate psalm of the Psalter, expressing total abandonment in the grave, directly applied to Christ's descent into the tomb and hades.

[^273]: The Epistle of Great Friday Vespers: 1 Corinthians 1:18–2:2 (selection 125). St. Paul's fundamental discourse on the theology of the Cross: the word of the Cross as the power and wisdom of God against the worldly wisdom of Greeks and the seeking of signs by Jews.

[^274]: Alleluia of Great Friday Vespers, Tone 1: Psalm 68:2, 21, 24 (LXX 68:1, 20, 23, *Спаси́ мѧ Бж҃е, ꙗ҆́кѡ внидо́ша во́ды до дꙋшѝ моеѧ̀*), the Messianic Passion psalm describing overwhelming waters, bitter reproach, and the blinding of persecutors.

[^275]: The Gospel of Great Friday Vespers: Matthew 27:1–38; Luke 23:39–43; Matthew 27:39–54; John 19:31–37; Matthew 27:55–61 (selection 110). A composite Passion Gospel harmonization spanning Christ's trial before Pilate, the suicide of Judas, the release of Barabbas, the crowning with thorns, the Crucifixion between two thieves, the repentance of the thief, the cosmic signs at His death, the piercing of His side, the deposition by Joseph of Arimathea, and the burial in the rock tomb opposite the women.

[^276]: Canonical 3-layer melodic model: Tone 2, Podoben: "When from the Tree" (*Є҆гда̀ ѿ дре́ва* / *Ὅτε ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου*), attributed to St. Theophanes Graptos. The famous Aposticha stichera of Great Friday Vespers depicting the burial of Christ by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus.

[^277]: Small Compline on Holy and Great Friday: prescribed to be recited in the cells (*въ ке́ллїахъ*), featuring the monumental Canon of the Crucifixion and the Lament of the Most Holy Theotokos (*Канѡ́нъ ѡ҆ Распѧ́тїи Гдⷭ҇ни, и҆ на пла́чь прест҃ы́ѧ Бцⷣы*).

[^278]: Authorship of the Lament of the Theotokos: attributed to Symeon the Metaphrast (Logothete, 10th century), one of the supreme masterpieces of Byzantine hymnographic mariology, meditating on the Mother of God's profound maternal grief, dialogue with her crucified and dead Son, and the promise of the Resurrection.

[^279]: Kontakion of the Lament of the Theotokos, Tone 2: *На́съ ра́ди Распѧ́таго прїиди́те всѝ воспои́мъ* ("Come, let us all hymn Him Who was crucified for our sake"). An epitome of the maternal grief of the Theotokos standing at Golgotha.

[^280]: Ikos of the Lament of the Theotokos: *Своего̀ А҆́гнца А҆́гница зрѧ́щи* ("Seeing her own Lamb drawn unto the slaughter..."). Reminiscent of the classical Kontakion of St. Romanos the Melodist on the Passion (*Mary at the Cross*), asking whether there is another marriage in Cana of Galilee.

[^281]: The Prayer of Compline to the Most Holy Theotokos by Paul the Monk of the Monastery of the Benefactress (Evergetis): *А҆́спиле, а҆мо́лѷнте, а҆́фѳоре, а҆́хранте, а҆́гнὴ Па́рѳене* (*Нескве́рнаѧ, небла́знаѧ, нетлѣ́ннаѧ, пречи́стаѧ, неискꙋсобра́чнаѧ* / "O Spotless, undefiled, incorrupt, immaculate, pure Virgin Bride of God").

[^282]: Codicological rubric: the Midnight Office of Holy and Great Saturday (*Полно́щницꙋ же пое́мъ въ ке́ллїахъ*) is read privately in the cells, without public ecclesiastical chanting, before the solemn nocturnal or dawn Matins of Holy Saturday.

[^283]: Codicological ornament: a decorative woodcut/typographical vignette depicting an ornamental scroll inscribed with the Greek letters Alpha and Omega and the cross (*A + Ω*), symbolizing Christ as the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End (Revelation 1:8, 22:13), placed at the conclusion of Great Friday Compline before Great Saturday.

[^284]: Codicological woodcut plate: A monumental woodcut headpiece engraving positioned at the opening of Holy and Great Saturday, depicting the Entombment of Christ (*Положе́нїе во гро́бъ* / *Epitaphios Threnos*). The dead Christ, wrapped in the winding-sheet (*плащани́ца*), is borne to the sepulchre by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, attended by the Virgin Theotokos, Saint John the Theologian, and the Myrrh-bearing women before a rock cave, flanked on both sides by quadruple vertical floral strapwork columns.

[^285]: Liturgical office opening: The Matins of Holy and Great Saturday (*Во святу́ю и вели́кую Суббо́ту на Ѹ҆́трени*), historically known as the Burial of Christ or the Lamentations at the Tomb (*Свяще́нный Пла́чь* / *Ἐπιτάφιος Θρῆνος*), one of the supreme climaxes of the Byzantine liturgical year.

[^286]: Liturgical time rubric: "At the seventh hour of the night" (*въ седмы́й ча́съ но́щи*), designating approx. 1:00 AM by Byzantine/monastic seasonal reckoning, prescribing that this service be celebrated as an all-night nocturnal vigil keeping watch over the buried Lord.

[^287]: The Resurrection and Entombment Troparia at "God is the Lord": The noble Joseph (*Благообра́зный І҆ѡ́сифъ*), When Thou didst descend unto death (*Е҆гда̀ снизше́лъ є҆сѝ къ сме́рти*), and Unto the myrrh-bearing women (*Мѵроно́сицамъ жена́мъ*), summarizing the mystery of the Crucified, buried, and descending Life-giver.

[^288]: Codicological rubric: The Parrecclesiarch (*Параекклисїа́рхъ* / candle-lighter and sacristan) distributes unlit or lighted candles to all the brethren, symbolizing the light of the Resurrection already dawning within the nocturnal darkness of the tomb.

[^289]: The Amomos / Kathisma 17 (*Блаже́ни непоро́чнїи* / Psalm 118): The longest psalm in the Psalter, the funeral psalm of the Hebrew and Christian traditions, interpreted typologically as the psalm of the spotless Lamb of God lying in the tomb.

[^290]: The Enkomia / Lamentations at the Tomb: Prescribed in three Staseis (*трѝ Статі̑и*). The First Stasis is chanted in Tone 5 (*гла́съ є҃*), the Second in Tone 2 (*гла́съ в҃*), and the Third in Tone 3 (*гла́съ г҃*). Each psalm verse is intercalated with a short hymnographic sticheron/troparion meditating on Christ's death and descent into hades.

[^291]: Rubric on the initial censing: The Superior (*И҆гꙋ́менъ*) stands before the Shroud (*Плащани́ца*) in the center of the nave (*посредѣ̀ Це́ркве*), sings the opening refrain, and censes cruciformly (*покади́въ крⷭ҇тоѡбра́знѡ*), followed by censing the altar and the whole church.

[^292]: Theological typology: Directly juxtaposing the messianic glory of Psalm 44:3 ("Fair in beauty beyond all the sons of men" / *Кра́сный добро́тою па́че всѣ́хъ человѣ́къ*) with the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53:2 ("He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see Him, there is no beauty" / *ꙗ҆́кѡ беззра́ченъ ме́ртвъ ꙗ҆влѧ́етсѧ*).

[^293]: Christ as the Rock of Life (*Живота̀ Ка́мень*): Evoking the miraculous rock struck in Horeb (Exodus 17:6, 1 Corinthians 10:4) and the stone cut out of the mountain without hands (Daniel 2:34, 45). Swallowing this living Rock, hades is forced to vomit up all the righteous dead held captive since Adam.

[^294]: Scriptural typology: The dying grain of wheat (*я́коже пшени́чное зе́рно*), echoing Christ's discourse in John 12:24 ("Truly, truly, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abides alone: but if it die, it brings forth much fruit"), by His death yielding an abundant harvest of resurrected souls.

[^295]: Pauline Adam-Christ typology: Christ as the New Adam (*но́вый во пло́ти ꙗ҆вле́йсѧ А҆да́мъ*), reversing the death brought by the first Adam through envy and disobedience (Romans 5:14-19, 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45).

[^296]: Messianic lion typology: The sleeping lion (*я́коже ле́въ ꙋ҆снꙋ́въ пло́тїю*), drawn from the patriarchal blessing of Jacob over Judah in Genesis 49:9 ("Judah is a lion's whelp; from the prey, my son, thou art gone up: he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as an old lion; who shall rouse him up?"), interpreted by the Fathers as Christ sleeping in the tomb in His humanity while invincible in His divinity.

[^297]: Patristic Eve-Church typology: As Eve was fashioned from the side of the sleeping Adam in Eden (Genesis 2:21-22), so the Church was born and the sacraments of water (Baptism) and blood (Eucharist) poured forth from the pierced side of Christ asleep on the Cross (John 19:34).

[^298]: Messianic imagery of Eden: The flaming sword placed at the gate of Paradise to guard the Tree of Life (Genesis 3:24) is blunted and turned back by the sacrifice of Christ, granting redeemed humanity re-entry into Eden.

[^299]: Hymnographic mariology: The Mother of God as the Ewe (*А҆́гница*) weeping over her Lamb (*А҆́гнецъ*) led to the slaughter, directly continuing the poetic paradigm of St. Romanos the Melodist's Kontakion *Mary at the Cross*.

[^300]: Physical witnesses of the Resurrection: The empty grave clothes—the linen winding-sheet (*плащани́ца* / *σινδών*) and the napkin that was about His head (*суда́рь* / *σουδάрион*, John 20:6-7)—left behind in the tomb as silent, irrefutable testimony against the slanders of the chief priests.

[^301]: Direct apostrophe to Judas Iscariot: Indicting his feigned concern for the poor at the anointing in Bethany (John 12:4-6) and his covetous betrayal of the uncontainable divine Myrrh for thirty pieces of silver.

[^302]: Christ as the Spiritual Rock: Drawing upon Numbers 20:11 and 1 Corinthians 10:4 ("and that Rock was Christ"), struck to pour forth living waters of salvation in the wilderness.

[^303]: The sacramental dual stream: The "two-fold river" (*сугу́бая рѣка́*) of blood and water flowing from Christ's pierced side (John 19:34), the font of Baptism and the cup of the Holy Eucharist granting immortal life.

[^304]: Second Stasis of the Praises (*Статїа втора́я*): Chanted in Tone 2 (*гла́съ в҃*), beginning with the left choir singing the opening refrain: "It is truly meet to magnify Thee, O Christ the Life-giver..." (*Досто́йно є҆́сть велича́ти тѧ̀, Живода́вче Хрⷭ҇тѐ*).

[^305]: Christ's Sabbath rest: Meditating upon the Lord's physical death as a "natural life-giving sleep" (*естественноживо́тный со́нъ*), wherein He rests on the Great Saturday from all His works of redemption, even as God rested on the seventh day from creation (Genesis 2:2-3, Hebrews 4:9-10).

[^306]: The Mother of God's sorrow: Contrasting her painless virginal birthgiving (*кромѣ̀ болѣ́зней*, preserving her perpetual virginity) with the excruciating maternal birth-pangs (*болѣ́зни нестерпи̑мыя*) endured at the foot of the Cross, fulfilling Simeon's prophecy (Luke 2:35).

[^307]: Cosmic signs: The rending of the temple veil from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51) and the darkening of the sun (Luke 23:44-45), signaling the passing of the Old Covenant and creation's shuddering at the burial of its Creator.

[^308]: The Paschal Salutation: Anticipating the risen Christ's first word to the Myrrh-bearing women in the garden: "Rejoice!" (*Χαίρετε* / *Ра́дуйтеся*, Matthew 28:9).

[^309]: Theological and patristic typology: The "twofold-sprouting grain, naturally living" (*Зе́рно двоєра́сленное, є҆стественножи́зненное*), sown in the depths of the earth with tears today (John 12:24), evoking Christ's divine and human natures (*διφυὲς σπέρμα*) dying according to the flesh to yield the immortal harvest of the Resurrection.

[^310]: Liturgical funeral hymnography: The "departure songs" or funeral hymns (*пѣ̑сни и҆схо́дныѧ* / *ἐξόδιοι ᾠδαί*), blended with lamentation, chanted by the noble Joseph of Arimathea as he reverently buries the Lord in his own new rock-hewn sepulchre (Matthew 27:59-60).

[^311]: Codicological and liturgical realism: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus anointing the sacred Body of Christ with a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39-40), an act celebrated as "newly meet" or "wondrously adorned" (*новолѣ́пнѡ*), causing the whole earth to shudder in astonishment.

[^312]: Scriptural stone typology: The radical antinomy of the "smoothed stone" covering the divine "Cornerstone" (*Ка́мень оу҆глажде́нный, краеꙋго́льный покрыва́етъ Ка́мень*), directly drawing upon Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 117:22, and 1 Peter 2:6, while mortal man covers God in the tomb.

[^313]: Eucharistic vine typology: Christ as the "Life-flowing Vine" (*живото́чнаѧ Лозо̀*), rooted in John 15:1 ("I am the true Vine"), cut down from the earth upon the Cross yet pouring forth the immortal wine of salvation for the life of the world.

[^314]: Irony of the Johannine temple saying: Direct apostrophe to the Jewish authorities concerning Christ's prophetic declaration: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19-21, Matthew 26:61), which they willfully used as an accusation to condemn Him.

[^315]: Patristic pelican typology: Christ figured forth as the pelican (*ꙗ҆́коже неѧ́сыть* / *ὥσπερ πελεκάν*) of ancient Christian bestiaries and Psalm 101:7, which pierces its own breast to revive its dead young with the outpoured life-streams of its own blood.

[^316]: Scriptural Joshua typology: Contrasting Joshua the son of Nun, who commanded the sun to stand still in the sky over Gibeon to slaughter the five kings (Joshua 10:12-13), with Jesus Christ the true Sun of Righteousness, Who concealed Himself in the tomb to overthrow the ruler of darkness and hades.

[^317]: Fulfillment of the Lucan prophecy: The Virgin Mary crying out in anguish at the foot of the Cross: "O woe! Simeon's prophecy is accomplished: for Thy sword hath passed through my heart, O Emmanuel" (Luke 2:35).

[^318]: Typology of the New Adam: The dual restoration wrought by Christ's Passion: His side pierced by the lance to heal the primeval wound of the rib whence Eve was taken, and His hands nailed to the wood of the Cross to undo the intemperate stretching forth of the hands of the first-parents toward the forbidden tree (Genesis 3:6).

[^319]: Scriptural lamentation typology: Evoking Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted because they are not (Jeremiah 31:15, Matthew 2:18), here surpassed by the choir of the disciples weeping alongside the Virgin Mother over the slain Son of God.

[^320]: Lviv Stauropegion recension variant: The imperial petition in the Trinity Troparion concluding the Second Stasis: "strengthen the sceptre of the Orthodox Emperor against adversaries" (*ски́птръ правосла́внагѡ І҆мпера́тора оу҆крѣпѝ на ра́тныѧ*), preserving the historic Austro-Hungarian state prayer for Emperor Franz Joseph I used across the Greek Catholic Metropolitanate of Galicia in the 1907 edition.

[^321]: Third Stasis of the Lamentations (*Статі́а тре́тїа*): Chanted in Tone 3 (*гла́съ г҃*), opening with the rapid, colometric stanza: "Every generation, O my Christ, offers a hymn unto Thy Burial" (*Ро́ди всѝ пѣ́снь Погребе́нїю твоемꙋ̀ прино́сѧтъ, Хрⷭ҇тѐ мо́й*), accompanied by a complete censing of the Epitaphios and the temple.

[^322]: Typological ingratitude of Israel: Juxtaposing the divine benevolence of the Exodus—feeding Israel with heavenly manna in the desert (Exodus 16)—with their bitter return, offering Christ gall and vinegar upon the Cross (Psalm 68:22, Matthew 27:34).

[^323]: Wisdom literature citation: Quoting the imagery of Solomon from Proverbs 22:14 and 23:27 ("a deep pit is the mouth of a strange woman / the transgressor"), here applied to the deceitful and murderous mouth of Judas and the false accusers.

[^324]: Patristic and poetic imagery of Springtime: The sorrowful maternal lament of the Theotokos apostrophizing Christ as her "sweetest Springtime" (*Ѡ҆ сладча́йшаѧ моѧ̀ Весно̀*), symbolizing the vernal rebirth of creation withered by winter and death, now mourning the departure of its light.

[^325]: Old Testament sacrificial typology: The Virgin Mary figured forth as the Heifer (*Ю҆́ница*) lamenting over the divine Calf (*Теле́цъ*) hung upon the Tree, drawing upon the Levitical heifer sacrifices (Numbers 19) and the prophet Hosea's sacrificial language.

[^326]: Exodus cloud pillar typology: Contrasting He Who of old covered the wandering people of Israel with a protective pillar of cloud (Exodus 13:21-22) with His willing submission to be nailed in helplessness to the wood of the Cross.

[^327]: Typological contrast of the Two Josephs: Contrasting Joseph the Betrothed, who of old fled into Egypt carrying the Infant Savior to preserve Him from Herod (Matthew 2:13-14), with Joseph of Arimathea, who now buries His lifeless Body in the rock tomb.

[^328]: Culmination of Psalm 118: The final verse of the Great Kathisma (Psalm 118:176: "I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek Thy servant; for I have not forgotten Thy commandments") directly capped by the communal petition for ecclesiastical peace and redemption through the Resurrection.

[^329]: The Resurrectional Evlogetaria (*Тропари̑ по Непоро́чнахъ* / *Εὐλογητάρια*): Chanted in Tone 5 with the psalm refrain "Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes" (Psalm 118:12), marking the liturgical threshold where nocturnal burial grief gives way to the first joyful announcement of the empty tomb.

[^330]: The angelic rhetorical question: The radiant Angel sitting within the tomb rebuking the Myrrh-bearing women: "Why mingle ye myrrh with compassionate tears, O disciples?" (Luke 24:5), commanding them to dry their tears and herald the Resurrection to the Apostles.

[^331]: Codicological and liturgical authorship of the Holy Saturday Canon: The rubric on fol. 153 explicitly identifies the composite authorship of the canon: the Heirmoi of Odes 1–5 were composed by Kassia the Nun (Kassiane, ca. 810–865), while the Troparia of Odes 1–5 were written by Mark the Monk, Bishop of Idrus (Hydrus/Otranto in Apulia, 10th c.); the Heirmoi and Troparia of Odes 6–9 were composed by St. Cosmas of Maiuma (ca. 675–752).

[^332]: Epigraphic alphabetic acrostic of the Holy Saturday Canon: In the Greek original and preserved in Cyrillic transliteration in the margins of the 1907 Lviv edition (*Каѝ Си́меронъ дѐ Са́ккатонъ ме́лпѡ ме́га*), the acrostic reads: *Καὶ σήμερον δὲ Σάββατον μέλπω μέγα* ("And today also, I sing the Great Sabbath"). Mark of Idrus fitted his troparia in Odes 1–5 to complete the acrostic begun by Kassia's heirmoi, while Cosmas of Maiuma included both heirmoi and troparia in the acrostic for Odes 6–9.

[^333]: Patristic Christology of the three-day death: The phrase "By the power of the better part, Thy soul was separated from the flesh" (*Си́лою лꙋ́чшагѡ... ѿ пло́ти дꙋша̀ твоѧ̀ раздѣли́сѧ*) reflects the classic teaching of St. John of Damascus (*Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith* III.27): in Christ's death, His human soul was separated from His human body, yet His divine hypostasis remained inseparably united both to His soul in hades and to His body in the tomb.

[^334]: Scriptural and dogmatic typology of incorruption: "for Thy flesh saw not corruption, O Master" (*пло́ть бо твоѧ̀ и҆стлѣ́нїа не ви́дѣ, Влⷣко*), directly citing Psalm 15:10 (LXX: *οὐδὲ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σου ἰδεῖν διαφθοράν*) and the Apostle Peter's Pentecost sermon (Acts 2:27, 31), asserting the bodily incorruption of Christ in the tomb prior to the Resurrection.

[^335]: Dogma of the indivisible Hypostatic Union: "even if Thy temple was dissolved at the time of the Passion, yet even so one was the hypostasis of Thy Divinity and Thy Flesh" (*а҆́ще бо и҆ разори́сѧ тво́й хра́мъ во вре́мѧ Стра́сти, но и҆ та́кѡ є҆ди́нъ бѣ̀ соста́въ Бж҃ества̀ и҆ Пло́ти твоеѧ̀*), affirming that the separation of soul and body on the Cross did not dissolve the one composite Hypostasis of the Word incarnate.

[^336]: The Synaxarion of Holy and Great Saturday: Composed by Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos (ca. 1256–1335) for the Triodion, presenting the theological contemplation of the mystical Sabbath rest of Christ in the sepulchre, parallel to God resting on the seventh day of the primeval creation (Genesis 2:2-3).

[^337]: Patristic soteriology refuting the Satanic ransom: The Synaxarion decisively rejects the notion that Christ's Blood was paid as a ransom to the devil (*Но ни Кро́ви же взѧ́тъ вра́гъ на́шъ дїа́волъ... ка́кѡ бо а҆́ще не то́чїю ѿ Бг҃а, но и҆ Бг҃а є҆го̀ разбо́йникъ дїа́волъ ꙗ҆́ти и҆мѧ́ше;*), affirming with St. Gregory the Theologian (*Oration 45.22*) that the sacrifice was offered solely to God the Father for human redemption.

[^338]: Acrostic structure in Cosmas's odes: In Odes 7 and 8, the letters *Т-Ѡ-Н* and *М-Є-Л-П-Ѡ* are printed in the margins to continue the acrostic: *Σάββατον μέλπω* ("I sing the Sabbath"), demonstrating that Cosmas incorporated his Heirmoi into the structural sequence of the acrostic.

[^339]: The Heirmos *Lament Me not, O Mother* (*Не рыда́й менѐ, Ма́ти* / *Μὴ ἐποδύρου μου Μῆτερ*): The poetic dialogue between Christ in the tomb and the Virgin Mary, which served as the liturgical and iconographic foundation for the celebrated icon of "Extreme Humility" (*Ἄκρα Ταπείνωσις*) across the Byzantine and Slavic traditions.

[^340]: Sabbath typology of the Creation and Redemption: The Doxastikon of Praises (*Дне́шнїй де́нь та́йнѡ, вели́кїй Мѡѷсе́й проѡбразова́ше*) directly connects Genesis 2:2-3 with Christ's bodily Sabbath rest in the tomb, inaugurating the eternal Sabbath (*σαββατισμός*, Hebrews 4:9-10) of the New Covenant.

[^341]: Liturgical rubric for the Great Doxology and Procession: In the Ruthenian and Byzantine usages, during the singing of the solemn slow Trisagion of the Great Doxology, the priest in full vestments with the deacon and servers carries the Epitaphios (Holy Shroud) and the Holy Gospel in procession around the temple, representing the burial procession of Christ to the tomb.

[^342]: Maternal lament and Simeon's prophecy: The Funeral Sticheron (*Стїхи́ра надгро́бнаѧ: Прїиди́те, ᲂу҆блажи́мъ І҆ѡ́сифа приснопа́мѧтнаго*) incorporates the sorrowful lament of the Mother of God recalling the prophecy of Righteous Simeon (Luke 2:35), concluding with the threefold veneration: "We worship Thy Sufferings, O Christ, and Thy holy Resurrection!"

[^343]: Old Testament resurrection typology: The reading of Ezekiel 37:1-14 (the vision of the dry bones in the valley brought to life by the breath of the Spirit) stands as the preeminent prophetic witness of the universal bodily resurrection, chanted at the climax of Holy Saturday Matins.

[^344]: Composite liturgical Epistle lectionary: The Epistle reading (pericope 123) ingeniously fuses 1 Corinthians 5:6-8 ("Purge out therefore the old leaven... for our Pascha, Christ, is sacrificed for us") with Galatians 3:13-14 ("Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the Law, being made a curse for us"), directly linking the Paschal sacrifice with the redemption from the curse of the tree.

[^345]: Paschaltide Lenten Hours rubric: The First Hour is sung immediately in the narthex following Matins, while the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours are aggregated simply in the narthex with the Beatitudes (*съ бл҃же́нными*) prior to the solemn afternoon Vespers and Liturgy of St. Basil the Great.

[^346]: Liturgical time and structure of Holy Saturday Vespers: The service is appointed for the tenth hour of the day (approximately 4:00 PM), marking the transition toward the Paschal night. It unites Vespers with the Divine Liturgy of St. Basil the Great.

[^347]: Sacerdotal vesting and Proskomedia timing: Unlike the typical Byzantine order where the Proskomedia is completed before the Liturgy begins, on Holy Saturday (as on the eve of the Nativity and Theophany) the Proskomedia is performed during the singing of "Lord, I have cried" while the deacon and concelebrants vest, allowing the extensive Old Testament readings to serve their ancient baptismal catechetical purpose.

[^348]: The Doxastikon of Holy Saturday (*Дне́шнїй де́нь та́йнѡ*): Attributed to the Studite or early Byzantine hymnographers, this hymn parallels Genesis 2:2-3 with Christ's Sabbath rest in the tomb, concluding with His return through the Resurrection to life and eternal glory.

[^349]: Sacerdotal Entrance with the Holy Gospel: Because the Liturgy of St. Basil the Great follows immediately after the Old Testament readings, the Little Entrance of the Liturgy is combined with the Vespers entrance, made with the Gospel Book rather than the censer.

[^350]: The Fifteen Old Testament Lections of Holy Saturday: The ancient Byzantine and Jerusalem cathedral rite appointed these extended readings during the paschal baptismal vigil, while the catechumens were being baptized, chrismated, and led in procession into the temple for the Paschal Eucharist.

[^351]: Typology of the Paschal Lamb: Exodus 12:46 prescribes that no bone of the Paschal lamb shall be broken, fulfilled at Christ's Crucifixion (John 19:36), establishing the central Paschal typology of Christ as the true Lamb of God.

[^352]: The Sign of the Prophet Jonah: Chanted in its entirety across chapters 1 through 4, the Book of Jonah serves as the preeminent Scriptural type of Christ's three-day burial and descent into hades, as declared by Christ Himself in Matthew 12:40.

[^353]: The Cessation of Manna and the Archistrategos: Joshua 5 prefigures the cessation of the Old Testament types (the manna) upon entering the Promised Land and eating the unleavened bread, followed by the Christophany of the Commander (Archistrategos) of the Host of the Lord, venerated by Joshua as holy ground (parallel to Exodus 3:5).

[^354]: The Canticle of Moses at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:1-19): Chanted antiphonally with the refrains "Let us sing unto the Lord: for He hath been gloriously glorified!" following the Sixth Reading, standing as the universal Christian canticle of baptismal illumination, resurrection victory over hades, and deliverance from spiritual Pharaoh.

[^355]: The Prophecy of Zephaniah on the Day of the Resurrection: In Zephaniah 3:8, the LXX text explicitly reads: *ὑπόμεινόν με, λέγει Κύριος, εἰς ἡμέραν ἀναστάσεώς μου εἰς μαρτύριον* ("Wait for Me, saith the Lord, unto the day of My resurrection as a witness"), celebrated as a direct prophetic witness of Christ's resurrection.

[^356]: Elijah, the Widow of Zarephath, and the Inexhaustible Cruse: The miracle of the jar of flour and the cruse of oil that did not fail, followed by the resurrection of the widow's son by Elijah breathing threefold upon him, serves as an Old Testament type of both the inexhaustible Eucharistic gifts and the universal resurrection from the dead.

[^357]: The Robe of Salvation and the Nuptial Joy of the Church: Isaiah 61:10–62:5 provides the baptismal vesting verse ("My soul shall rejoice in the Lord: for He hath clothed me with the robe of salvation...") and celebrates the mystical marriage of the Church, redeemed and adorned for her Bridegroom.

[^358]: The Binding of Isaac (the Akedah): Genesis 22:1–15 stands as the supreme Old Testament sacrifice prefiguring the Father offering His Only-begotten Son on the Cross, carrying the wood of the sacrifice to Mount Moriah (Golgotha), and the ram caught in the thicket by its horns sparing Isaac.

[^359]: The Eleventh Reading: from the Prophecy of Isaiah (Isaiah 61:1-9) — The Messianic Anointing of the Servant of the Lord. Proclaimed by Christ Himself in the synagogue of Nazareth (Luke 4:18-19) as fulfilled in His person, this lection heralds the Paschal transformation from mourning to jubilation ("glory instead of ashes, the anointing of joy to the mourners") and the restoration of the everlasting covenant through the holy priesthood of the new dispensation.

[^360]: The Twelfth Reading: from the Fourth Book of Kings (4 Kings 4:8-37 [2 Kings 4:8-37]) — Elisha and the Resurrection of the Shunammite's Son. The miraculous conception granted to the barren woman, followed by the bodily resurrection of her deceased child through the prophet stretching himself upon him and breathing seven times upon him, prefigures the descent of Christ into hades and His vivification of fallen Adam and all mortal flesh.

[^361]: The Thirteenth Reading: from the Prophecy of Isaiah (Isaiah 63:11–64:5) — The Prophetic Invocation of the Divine Arm and the Rendition of the Heavens. The prophet recalls the exodus of Israel through the Red Sea by the right hand of Moses, invoking the Fatherhood of God ("Thou, O Lord, art our Father, our Redeemer: from the beginning Thy name is upon us") and imploring Him to rend the heavens and descend with consuming fire upon the adversaries.

[^362]: The Fourteenth Reading: from the Prophecy of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 31:31-34) — The New Covenant Written upon the Heart. Foretelling the transition from the external Sinai covenant to the internal sacramental economy of grace, the Lord promises to write His divine laws directly upon the hearts and minds of His people, culminating in the remission of all transgressions through Christ's voluntary sacrifice.

[^363]: The Fifteenth Reading: from the Prophecy of Daniel (Daniel 3:1-56/88) — The Three Youths in the Babylonian Furnace. Chanted at the conclusion of the baptismal lections, the preservation of Ananias, Azarias, and Misael unburned amidst the raging flames by the Angel of the Lord constitutes the supreme Old Testament type of Christ's descent into hades, descending into the fiery realm of death without suffering corruption, while delivering the righteous from eternal fire.

[^364]: The Canticle of the Three Youths (*Бл҃гослови́те всѧ̑ дѣла̀ Гдⷭ҇нѧ* / Daniel 3:57-88): The ancient *Benedicite*, chanted antiphonally between reader and choir while all stand ("We stand here, and sing"), uniting all orders of the cosmos—angels, heavens, waters, celestial luminaries, elements, and the spirits of the just—in the cosmic doxology anticipating the Paschal dawn.

[^365]: The Baptismal Anthem (*Е҆ли́цы во Хрⷭ҇та̀ крести́стесѧ* / Galatians 3:27): Substituted for the Trisagion on Holy Saturday, recalling the historical celebration of the Paschal baptism of the catechumens during the 15 Old Testament readings, after which the newly illumined were led in procession into the temple clad in white robes for the Eucharistic Liturgy.

[^366]: The Epistle of Holy Saturday (Romans 6:3-11, pericope 91): St. Paul's classic theological locus on Holy Baptism as sacramental co-burial and co-resurrection with Christ, asserting that as Christ died unto sin once and lives unto God, the baptized are dead unto sin and alive unto God in Christ Jesus.

[^367]: The Prokeimenon Anthem of Tone 7 (*Воскреснѝ Бж҃е, сꙋдѝ землѝ* / Psalm 81:8 [82:8]): Replacing the customary Alleluia, this triumphant refrain with the verses of Psalm 81 is sung while the sacred ministers divest themselves of their dark Lenten vestments in the sanctuary and vest in white and radiant robes, while the dark paraments of the holy table and church are replaced with bright white coverings.

[^368]: The Gospel of the Resurrection (Matthew 28:1-20, pericope 115): The first liturgical reading of the Resurrection of Christ, narrating the dawn at the sepulchre, the earthquake, the descent of the Angel rolling back the stone, the fear of the guards, the appearance of the Risen Christ to the women, and the universal apostolic commission on the mountain in Galilee.

[^369]: The Cherubic Hymn of Holy Saturday (*Да молчи́тъ вся́каѧ пло́ть человѣ́ча* / Tone 8): Borrowed from the ancient Jerusalem Liturgy of Saint James, this troparion replaces the standard Byzantine *Cherubikon* (*И҆́же херꙋві́мы*), bidding all earthly creation to be silent as the King of kings and Lord of lords comes forth to be slain and given as spiritual food to the faithful, preceded by the celestial hosts.

[^370]: The Blessing of Bread and Wine at the Analoy: Because the Liturgy concluded late in the evening and the faithful remained in church for the vigil leading to midnight Paschal Matins, bread, wine, dates, and figs were blessed upon an analoy in the nave to sustain the worshippers during the reading of the Acts of the Apostles.

[^371]: Reader's Service Rubric for Vespers: When the Divine Liturgy cannot be celebrated due to dire necessity, the Typikon directs the office to conclude as standard Vespers with the Resurrection Aposticha Stichera in Tone 1 from the Oktoechos, preserving the complete hymnographic witness of the Resurrection.

[^372]: The Nocturnal Vigil and the Reading of the Acts of the Apostles: The Typikon specifies that the Liturgy must conclude at the second hour of the night (approx. 8:00 PM). The Slavonic rubric notes the Greek practice where the brethren remain continuously in church, partaking of the blessed bread and wine while the reader begins the continuous reading of the Acts of the Apostles (*Дѣя́нїа ст҃ы́хъ а҆пⷭ҇лъ*).

[^373]: The Canon of Holy Saturday Compline by Symeon Metaphrastes (the Logothete): Entitled "On the Bodily Burial of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and on the Lamentation of the Most Holy Theotokos" in Tone 6. The rubric notes that this office and canon are absent from the Greek Triodion, which omits Compline on Holy Saturday evening, witnessing to a distinct Slavic liturgical development.

[^374]: The Lamentation of the Theotokos at the Burial of Christ: Sharing its Heirmoi with the Great Saturday Matins Canon ("He Who in ancient times concealed..."), the troparia of this canon present the maternal grief of the Virgin Mary standing before the Cross, pleading with Joseph of Arimathea to approach Pilate and bury the Body of her Son.

[^375]: Ode 6 Heirmos of Holy Saturday Compline: "Jonah was caught, but not held fast..." In this heirmos, the Prophet Jonah's three-day deliverance from the belly of the sea monster prefigures Christ's bodily rest in the tomb and His triumph over death. The concluding phrase quotes Jonah 2:9 (LXX: "They that observe vanities and lies have forsaken their own mercy"), addressed here directly to the Roman guard ("custodia") keeping watch over Christ's sepulchre.

[^376]: The Holy Saturday Kontakion and Ikos in Tone 6: "He Who shut the abyss is beheld dead..." Traditionally ascribed to Saint Romanos the Melodist, this hymn contemplates the supreme theological antinomy of the Creator resting bodily in the tomb while hades groans below and the Jews plot to slander His Resurrection. The refrain proclaims Holy Saturday as the "most blessed Sabbath" (prefigured in Genesis 2:2-3), wherein Christ rests from all His works of recreation.

[^377]: The Continuous Reading of the Acts of the Apostles: Preserving the ancient Jerusalem nocturnal vigil before Paschal Matins, the Typikon directs that after Compline the reader immediately begins reading the Acts of the Apostles, the biblical account of the Resurrection proclaimed to the nations, continuing until the fourth hour of the night (approx. 10:00 PM) when the bells are struck for the Paschal Midnight Office.

[^378]: The Paschal Midnight Office (Nocturns): Celebrated late on Saturday night before the midnight Paschal vigil, the Midnight Office comprises the repetition of the Great Saturday Matins Canon ("He Who in ancient times concealed the pursuing tyrant...", Tone 6). During Ode 9, the clergy transfer the Holy Shroud (Plashchanytsia) from the tomb in the center of the nave to the holy table in the sanctuary, where it remains for forty days until the Apodosis of Pascha.

[^379]: The Paschal Patristic Homily of Saint Epiphanius of Cyprus: Entitled *In sancto et magno Sabbato* (PG 43:439-464), this classic patristic lection opens with the renowned words: "What is this? Today there is a great silence upon the earth, a great silence and stillness, for the King sleeps." It portrays Christ descending into hades to awaken Adam and Eve and all the righteous of the Old Covenant.

[^380]: The Extended Litany at the Midnight Office: Includes seasonal agricultural petitions according to weather conditions (supplications for rain during drought or for temperate dry weather during unseasonable rains), reflecting the ancient agrarian liturgical cycle embedded in the Slavic Trebnik and Typikon traditions.

[^381]: The Concluding Dismissal of the Holy Saturday Midnight Office: The final liturgical dismissal of the Lenten Triodion period, commemorating Christ Who "voluntarily was laid in the grave in the Flesh and trod down hades." Immediately following this dismissal, the church lights are extinguished in anticipation of the Paschal midnight procession.

[^382]: The Frontispiece Engraving of the Resurrection of Christ (p206): Designed and executed after a sketch under the direction of Evlogy (E. V.) Voronets in 1901 for the Stauropegion typography, this full-page plate depicts the triumphant Risen Christ ascending above the open tomb surrounded by radiant beams of light and angelic choirs, with the biblical caption from Luke 24:34: "Truly the Lord is risen..."

[^383]: The Master Inscription of the Pentecostarion: "Beginning with God the Holy. The Pentecostarion, that is, the Festal Fifty Days..." This formal incipit marks the boundary between the Lenten Triodion (which concluded with the Midnight Office) and the Pentecostarion proper, which encompasses the liturgical period from the dawn of Holy Pascha through the Sunday of All Saints.

[^384]: The Paschal Midnight Procession and Outdoor Matins Opening: At midnight the church bells peal, the temple is filled with incense, and the clergy and faithful process out of the dark sanctuary through the northern doors into the narthex (or outside around the temple) with tapers, icons, and the Holy Gospel, while chanting the Sticheron in Tone 6 ("Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior..."). The western doors are shut to symbolize the sealed sepulchre of Christ.

[^385]: The Paschal Troparion in Tone 5: "Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and upon those in the tombs bestowing life." Chanted for the first time before the closed doors of the temple, this core hymnographic proclamation is repeated three times by the superior and three times by the choir, inaugurating the bright Paschal celebration.

[^386]: The Paschal Verses: Drawn from Psalm 67:1-3 [68:1-3] ("Let God arise, and let His enemies be scattered...") and Psalm 117:24 [118:24] ("This is the day which the Lord hath made..."), these verses are chanted antiphonally between the superior and the choir before the temple doors are struck with the Cross and flung open, symbolizing Christ shattering the gates of brass and breaking the bars of iron in hades.

[^387]: The Paschal Canon of Saint John of Damascus in Tone 1: Known as the "Golden Canon" or the "Queen of Canons," this hymnographic masterpiece of the 8th century is celebrated with dynamic censing of the whole temple and mutual Paschal greetings ("Christ is risen! Truly He is risen!") at every ode, accompanied by the repeated refrain "Christ is risen from the dead."

[^388]: The Paschal Hypakoe in Tone 4: "When they that were with Mary came before the dawn..." Commemorating the holy Myrrh-Bearing Women arriving at the sepulchre before the dawn, where the angel announces to them that Christ is risen and bids them proclaim the glad tidings to the Apostles.

[^389]: The Paschal Reading from Saint Gregory the Theologian: Oration 45 (The Second Paschal Oration, PG 36:623-664), opening with the citation of Habakkuk 2:1: "Upon my watch will I stand, and sit upon the rock..." The prophet Habakkuk stands upon his watch, beholding the light-bearing angel proclaiming the Resurrection of Christ.

[^390]: The Paschal Kontakion in Tone 8: "Though Thou didst descend into the grave, O Immortal One..." Ascribed to Saint Romanos the Melodist, this hymn crystallizes the dogma of the Resurrection: Christ's bodily descent into the grave destroyed the dominion of hades, while His rising brought the apostolic greeting of joy ("Rejoice!") to the Myrrh-Bearers and divine peace to the disciples.

[^391]: The Paschal Synaxarion for the Holy and Great Sunday of Pascha, traditionally attributed to Nikephoros Kallistos Xanthopoulos (c. 1256–1335). It expounds the Hebrew etymology of "Pascha" as "passage" (transitus / διαβατήρια), harmonizes the four resurrectional Gospel accounts of the appearances to the Myrrh-Bearing Women and Apostles, and presents two distinct liturgical computations for Christ's "three days in the tomb" (the triduum) based on the Hebrew reckoning of a day-and-night (nychthemeron).

[^392]: The ancient resurrectional hymn *Resurrectionem Christi cernentes* (Воскресе́нїе Хрⷭ҇то́во ви́дѣвше). Unlike throughout the rest of the liturgical year where it is chanted once during Sunday Matins, during the Paschal season it is chanted three times in succession at Matins, at the Paschal Hours, and at the Paschal Typika.

[^393]: Ode 7 Heirmos of the Paschal Canon: "He Who delivered the youths from the furnace..." (Ѻ҆́троки ѿ пе́щи И҆зба́вивый). Based on the Song of the Three Holy Children in the Babylonian furnace (Daniel 3), this hymn contemplates the supreme mystery of the Incarnation: Christ, clothed in our human nature, voluntarily undergoes mortal suffering in order to vest our mortality with the beauty of incorruption.

[^394]: Ode 8 Heirmos of the Paschal Canon: "This chosen and holy day..." (Се́й нарече́нный и҆ ст҃ы́й де́нь). Echoing Gregory the Theologian's Paschal Oration, this hymn proclaims the Day of the Resurrection as the "one of the Sabbaths" (mia ton sabbaton), the King and Lord of days, the "Feast of feasts and Triumph of triumphs."

[^395]: The Paschal Ode 9 Megalynarion: "The angel cried aloud unto Her that is full of grace..." (А҆́ггелъ вопїѧ́ше Бл҃года́тнѣй). This renowned ninth-ode refrain combines the Archangel Gabriel's greeting to the Mother of God with the joyful announcement of the third-day Resurrection of Her Son, bidding the human race to rejoice in the destruction of death.

[^396]: Ode 9 Heirmos of the Paschal Canon: "Shine, shine, O New Jerusalem..." (Свѣти́сѧ свѣти́сѧ но́вый І҆ерꙋсали́ме). Drawing upon Isaiah 60:1 ("Arise, shine, for thy light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee") and Revelation 21:2, this triumphant hymn celebrates the Church as the New Jerusalem and calls upon the Mother of God to exult in the bodily rising of Her Son.

[^397]: The Paschal Exapostilarion *Carne cum obdormivisses* (Пло́тїю оу҆сну́въ ꙗ҆́кѡ ме́ртвъ), an Automelon (having its own unique melody, traditionally assigned to Tone 3). It employs the poetic scriptural idiom of sleep for Christ's voluntary bodily death in the sepulchre, through which the forefather Adam is raised and mortality abolished.

[^398]: The Paschal Stichera in Tone 5: "A sacred Pascha is revealed unto us today..." (Па́сха свѧще́ннаѧ на́мъ дне́сь показа́ся). Traditionally ascribed to Saint John of Damascus, these festive troparia are intercalated with the prophetic verses of Psalm 67 [68], concluding with the majestic Paschal Doxasticon ("It is the day of Resurrection...") commanding universal reconciliation and mutual forgiveness in the light of Christ's victory.

[^399]: The Paschal Kiss of Peace and Rite of Mutual Forgiveness (Цѣлова́нїе). Standing before the holy doors, the superior, clergy, monastic brethren, workmen, and laity exchange the joyful Paschal greeting ("Christ is risen! Truly He is risen!"), venerating the precious Cross, the Holy Gospel, and the icons, embodying in liturgical action the spiritual pardon proclaimed in the Doxasticon: "Let us forgive all things by the Resurrection."
