[^2743]: Physical leaf p604 corresponds to printed folio 598 (`ф҃чи`). Matins continues after the Kathisma readings with resurrectional Sessional Hymns in Tone 8 and the standing Theotokion *Ѡ҆ тебѣ̀ ра́дꙋетсѧ*.

[^2744]: The melodic model *Tone 8, Podoben: "That which was commanded mystically" (Повелѣ́нное та́йнѡ)* corresponds to the canonical Greek automelon incipit *Τὸ προσταχθὲν μυστικῶς* / *Повелѣ́нное та́йнѡ*.

[^2745]: The melodic model *Tone 8, Podoben: "The Wisdom and Word of God" (Премꙋ́дрости Сло́ва)* corresponds to the canonical incipit *Τὴν Σοφίαν καὶ Λόγον* / *Премꙋ́дрости сло́ва*.

[^2746]: The rubric explicitly directs that *Ѡ҆ тебѣ̀ ра́дꙋетсѧ* ("All creation rejoices in thee"), composed by St. John of Damascus, be sung standing (*не сѣда́юще пое́мъ, но стоя́ще*), with fear and reverence, honoring its exalted status.

[^2747]: The Tone 8 Hypakoe *Мѵроно́сицы Жизнода́вца* recounts the encounter of the Myrrh-bearing women with the angel at the empty tomb.

[^2748]: Physical leaf p605 corresponds to printed folio 599 (`ф҃чѳ`). The complete four Antiphons of the Hymns of Ascents (Anabathmoi) in Tone 8 are chanted. Tone 8 uniquely contains four Antiphons instead of the customary three found in Tones 1 through 7.

[^2749]: The first Antiphon of Tone 8 draws upon Psalm 128:1-2 (LXX), likening the haters of Zion to withered grass.

[^2750]: Antiphon 2 meditates on holy fear guarding against pride, and the final judgment by fire and torment.

[^2751]: Antiphon 3 invokes the tripartite theology of the Trinity (*Бг҃осло́вїе є҆ди́ница трист҃а́ѧ*): the unoriginate Father, the timelessly begotten Son, and the co-enthroned Holy Spirit.

[^2752]: Antiphon 4 cites Psalm 132:1 (LXX) ("Behold now, what is good or what is pleasant? But that brethren dwell together") and Christ's words regarding the lilies of the field (Matthew 6:28).

[^2753]: Physical leaf p606 corresponds to printed folio 600 (`х`). Sunday Matins proceeds with the Prokeimenon, the 1st Resurrection Gospel (Matthew 28:16-20, Pericope 116), and the canon complex comprising 4 canons.

[^2754]: The rubric notes that from this Sunday of All Saints, the eleven weekly Resurrection Matins Gospels (*Є҆ѵⷢлїа воскр҃сна*) begin to be read in regular sequential cycle (*по ря́дꙋ*).

[^2755]: The heirmos of Ode 1 in Tone 8 *Колесницегони́телѧ фараѡ́нѧ* ("Pharaoh the charioteer") is the classical Resurrection heirmos based on the Song of Moses (Exodus 15:1-19).

[^2756]: The Cross-Resurrectional Canon (*Канѡ́нъ Крⷭ҇товоскре́сенъ*) uses the heirmos *Во́дꙋ проше́дъ* ("Having traversed the water"), focusing on Christ's harrowing of Hades and the exaltation of human nature upon the Father's throne.

[^2757]: Physical leaf p607 corresponds to printed folio 601 (`ха`). Ode 1 concludes with the Canon of All Saints, carrying the Greek alphabetical acrostic: *Τῶν ἁγίων πάντων πολυώνυμα τάγματα μέλπω* ("I sing the multifold ranks of all the saints").

[^2758]: The Katavasia for the Canons is taken from the Canon of the Annunciation/Akathist: *Ѡ҆тве́рзꙋ оу҆ста̀ моѧ̑* ("I shall open my mouth"), which serves as the general Katavasia throughout the liturgical year outside festive periods.

[^2759]: The heirmos of Ode 3 in Tone 8 *Оу҆твержде́й въ нача́лѣ нб҃са̀* ("Thou Who in the beginning didst establish the heavens") is based on the Canticle of Hannah (1 Kingdoms / 1 Samuel 2:1-10 LXX).

[^2760]: Physical leaf p608 corresponds to printed folio 602 (`хв`). Ode 3 of the canons concludes, followed by the Sessional Hymns of All Saints in Tone 8.

[^2761]: The Cross-Resurrectional heirmos *Нбⷭ҇нагѡ крꙋ́га верхотво́рче* ("Fashioner of the vault of heaven") and Theotokion heirmos *Ты̀ є҆сѝ оу҆твержде́нїе* ("Thou art the establishment") complete the intermediate canons of Ode 3.

[^2762]: In the Canon of All Saints, Ode 3 continues the acrostic with letters I, Ω, N, and Π, praising the holy pastors, teachers, and assemblies of righteous virgins.

[^2763]: The Sessional Hymn in Tone 8 *Пра́ѻтецъ, Ѻ҆тє́цъ, Патрїа́рхъ* ("Celebrating the holy memory of Thy Forefathers, Fathers, Patriarchs...") serves as a comprehensive liturgical litany of all orders of sanctity.

[^2764]: Physical leaf p609 corresponds to printed folio 603 (`хг`). Ode 4 of the canons begins with the Resurrection heirmos *Ты̀ моѧ̀ крѣ́пость Гдⷭ҇и* ("Thou art my strength, O Lord"), based on the Canticle of Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3:1-19 LXX).

[^2765]: The Marian troparion invokes the Virgin as the "untilled field" (*неѡра́ннаѧ Ни́во*) that brought forth the life-bearing ear of wheat (*кла́съ животво́рный*), echoing patristic Eucharistic typology.

[^2766]: In the Canon of All Saints, Ode 4 incorporates the letters Α, N, and T of the acrostic, praising the hieromartyrs and ascetic fathers who overcame carnal impulses.

[^2767]: Physical leaf p610 corresponds to printed folio 604 (`хд`). Ode 4 concludes with the letters Ω and N, followed by Ode 5 of the four canons.

[^2768]: The heirmos of Ode 5 in Tone 8 *Вскꙋ́ю мѧ̀ ѿри́нꙋлъ є҆сѝ* ("Why hast Thou cast me off from Thy face") is based on the Canticle of Isaiah (Isaiah 26:9-20).

[^2769]: The Cross-Resurrectional troparion highlights Christ being clothed in mocking purple before His Passion, thereby clothing the shameful nakedness of fallen Adam.

[^2770]: In the Canon of All Saints, Ode 5 begins with the letters Π and O of the acrostic word *ΠΟΛΥΩΝΥΜΑ*, commemorating the Old Testament patriarchs and prophets who foresaw Christ before the giving of the Mosaic Law.

[^2771]: Physical leaf p611 corresponds to printed folio 605 (`х҃є`). Ode 5 of the Canon of All Saints concludes with the letters Λ and Y of the Greek acrostic, followed by Ode 6 of the four canons.

[^2772]: The Resurrectional heirmos of Ode 6 in Tone 8 *Ѡ҆чи́сти мѧ̀ Сп҃се* ("Cleanse me, O Savior") reflects Jonah's prayer from the belly of the sea monster (Jonah 2:3-10 LXX).

[^2773]: The Cross-Resurrectional troparion highlights Christ stretching out His hands upon the Cross to heal the unrestrained reaching forth of Adam's hand in Eden (Genesis 3:6).

[^2774]: In the Canon of All Saints, Ode 6 begins with the letter Ω of the acrostic word *ΠΟΛΥΩΝΥΜΑ*, meditating on Christ as the precious cornerstone laid in Sion (Isaiah 28:16, 1 Peter 2:6).

[^2775]: Physical leaf p612 corresponds to printed folio 606 (`х҃ѕ`). Ode 6 of All Saints concludes with the letters N, Y, and M, followed by the Kontakion and Ikos of All Saints in Tone 8 and the reading of the Synaxarion.

[^2776]: The Kontakion of All Saints in Tone 8 *Ꙗ҆́кѡ нача́тки є҆стества̀* ("As the first-fruits of nature, the universe offers unto Thee, O Lord, the God-bearing Martyrs") is attributed to St. Romanos the Melodist, serving as one of the most famous kontakia of the Byzantine liturgical year.

[^2777]: The Synaxarion for the Sunday of All Saints expounds three theological reasons why the Church established this feast immediately following Holy Pentecost: first, to demonstrate the universal fruit of the Holy Spirit's descent; second, to honor the countless anonymous saints whose names are known only to God across all lands; and third, to unite all the righteous into one common celebration since they struggled in one Christ.

[^2778]: Physical leaf p613 corresponds to printed folio 607 (`х҃з`). The Synaxarion recounts the historical dedication of the Church of All Saints in Constantinople by Emperor Leo VI the Wise (886–912) and provides an overview of the Triodion's liturgical journey from the fall of Adam to the heavenly gathering of all the saints.

[^2779]: Emperor Leo VI originally intended to dedicate the grand church to his pious first wife, Empress Theophano (d. 893/897), but when the Church hierarchy objected to immediate imperial canonization, Leo wisely dedicated the temple to All Saints of the whole world, noting: "Even if Theophano is holy, let her be numbered with all the saints."

[^2780]: The nine ranks of sanctity enumerated in the Synaxarion mirror the nine celestial angelic choirs: Forefathers, Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs, Hierarchs, Hieromartyrs and Venerable Martyrs, Venerables and Righteous, and holy Women, with the Most Holy Theotokos exalted above all creation.

[^2781]: The Resurrectional heirmos of Ode 7 in Tone 8 *Бж҃їѧ снизхожде́нїа* ("God's condescension") is based on the Canticle of the Three Holy Children in the Babylonian furnace (Daniel 3:26-56 LXX).

[^2782]: Physical leaf p614 corresponds to printed folio 608 (`х҃и`). Ode 7 of the Canon of All Saints incorporates the letters T, A, Γ, M, A, T, A of the acrostic phrase *ΤΑΓΜΑΤΑ ΜΕΛΠΩ* ("I sing the ranks"), followed by Ode 8 of the four canons.

[^2783]: The Resurrectional heirmos of Ode 8 in Tone 8 *Седмери́цею пе́щь* ("The Chaldean tyrant furiously heated the furnace sevenfold") continues the hymnography of Daniel 3:57-88 LXX (The Song of the Three Children).

[^2784]: The Trinitarian troparion of Ode 8 articulates the orthodox dogma of the one uncreated essence (*є҆диноесте́ственно*) and three distinct Hypostases (*трїѵпоста́снагѡ є҆стества̀*): the unoriginate Father, the co-essential Word, and the co-reigning Spirit of one essence.

[^2785]: The Marian troparion implores the Virgin to quench the fiery darts of the adversary (Ephesians 6:16).

[^2786]: Physical leaf p615 corresponds to printed folio 609 (`х҃ѳ`). Ode 8 of All Saints concludes with the letters M, E, Λ, and Π, followed by the Magnificat rubric and Ode 9 of the Resurrectional and festive canons.

[^2787]: The troparion of All Saints in Ode 8 affirms that by communion with God's deifying energies and illumination by His uncreated light, the saints become "gods by grace" through drawing near unto God (*бо́зи быва́ете, къ Бг҃ꙋ приближе́нїемъ*), reflecting classical patristic theosis (divinization; cf. Psalm 81:6 LXX, John 10:34-35).

[^2788]: The Resurrectional heirmos of Ode 9 in Tone 8 *Оу҆жасе́ся ѡ҆ се́мъ нб҃о* ("Heaven was dismayed thereat") is based on the Canticle of the Theotokos (Magnificat, Luke 1:46-55) and Jeremiah 2:12 LXX.

[^2789]: The Christological troparion of Ode 9 confesses Christ in two natures unconfusedly and indivisibly united (*во двою̀ сꙋщество̀ нераздѣ́льнѡ и҆ неслїѧ́ннѡ*), directly expressing the Chalcedonian dogmatic definition.

[^2790]: Physical leaf p616 corresponds to printed folio 610 (`х҃і`). Ode 9 concludes with the final troparia of All Saints (letters E, Λ, Π, and Ω, completing the acrostic *Τῶν ἁγίων πάντων πολυώνυμα τάγματα μέλπω*), the Katavasia of the Akathist, and the first Sunday Resurrectional Exapostilarion.

[^2791]: The Katavasia of Ode 9 *Вся́къ земноро́дный* ("Let every earth-born mortal leap for joy, enlightened in spirit") is taken from the Canon of the Annunciation / Akathist Hymn (Tone 4).

[^2792]: The 1st Resurrectional Exapostilarion *Со оу҆чени́ки взы́демъ на го́рꙋ Галїле́йскꙋю* ("Let us go up with the disciples into the mountain of Galilee") corresponds to the 1st Matins Gospel reading (Matthew 28:16-20), recalling Christ's Great Commission to baptize all nations in the name of the Holy Trinity.

[^2793]: Physical leaf p617 corresponds to printed folio 611 (`х҃аі`). Matins proceeds with the Exapostilarion of All Saints, its Theotokion, and the Praises (Lauds, *На хвали́техъ*), comprising 4 Resurrectional stichera in Tone 8, 1 Anatolian sticheron in Tone 8, and 3 stichera of All Saints in Tone 4.

[^2794]: The Exapostilarion of All Saints *Крⷭ҇ти́телѧ и҆ Предте́чꙋ* ("The Baptist and Forerunner, the Apostles, Prophets...") is chanted to the melodic model *Tone 2, Podoben: "Give ear, ye women" (Жены̀ оу҆слы́шите)*, although the incipit of the automelon is omitted in the printed heading of the 1907 edition.

[^2795]: The melodic model *Tone 4, Podoben: "As one valiant among martyrs" (Ꙗ҆́кѡ до́блѧ)* corresponds to the canonical Greek automelon *Ὡς γενναῖον ἐν μάρτυσιν*, sung for the praises of the holy martyrs and righteous ones.

[^2796]: Physical leaf p618 corresponds to printed folio 612 (`х҃в`). Matins concludes with the final sticheron of All Saints, the 1st Matins Gospel Doxasticon in Tone 1 *На го́рꙋ Оу҆ченикѡ́мъ и҆дꙋ́щымъ*, the Great Doxology, and the First Hour with the Catechesis of St. Theodore the Studite; followed by the opening of the Divine Liturgy.

[^2797]: The 1st Matins Gospel Doxasticon in Tone 1 *На го́рꙋ Оу҆ченикѡ́мъ и҆дꙋ́щымъ* ("Unto the disciples going into the mountain...") is the work of Emperor Leo VI the Wise, meditating on Christ's Ascension and the promise of His perpetual presence.

[^2798]: At the Divine Liturgy of All Saints, the Beatitudes (Makarismoi) are taken from Tone 8 (4 troparia) and from Ode 6 of the Canon of All Saints (4 troparia).

[^2799]: The Epistle for the Sunday of All Saints is Hebrews 11:33–12:2 (Pericope 330), recounting the heroic faith and sufferings of the Old Testament saints and martyrs who "through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises."

[^2800]: Physical leaf p619 corresponds to printed folio 613 (`х҃гї`). The Divine Liturgy concludes with the Gospel according to Matthew 10:32-33, 37-38; 19:27-30 (Pericope 38), the Communion Hymn (LXX Ps 148:1 and 32:1), and a rubric governing the celebration when a temple is dedicated to All Saints, featuring a woodcut engraving of the Mother of God and Child.

[^2801]: The rubric notes that at the agape meal (*на трапе́зѣ*), consolation is given to the brethren in anticipation of the Apostles' Fast (*гото́вѧщымся къ по́стномꙋ по́двигꙋ*), which customarily begins on the Monday following All Saints Sunday (or the second Monday after Pentecost in ancient Ruthenian monastic Typika).

[^2802]: For a parish or monastery dedicated to All Saints, the Typikon directs a full Vigil service with Polyeleos, Megalynarion (*Велича́емъ ва́съ А҆́пⷭ҇ли*), and Selected Psalm (LXX Ps 111:1 *Бл҃же́нъ мꙋ́жъ боя́йся Гдⷭ҇а*).

[^2803]: The woodcut engraving depicts the Most Holy Mother of God holding the divine Infant Christ in an oval mandorla of glory, symbolizing the Church of the Firstborn who surround the Queen of Heaven.

[^2804]: Physical leaf p620 corresponds to printed folio 614 (`х҃ді`). Opening of the Office of the Feast of the Most Holy Mystery of the Eucharist (Corpus Christi), celebrated on Thursday after the Sunday of All Saints, adorned with an elaborate headpiece engraving of the Eucharistic mystery.

[^2805]: The celebration of the Feast of the Most Holy Eucharist (Corpus Christi / *Боже́ственнаго Тѣ́ла*) on the Thursday following All Saints Sunday is a distinctive monument of the Ruthenian Greco-Catholic liturgical recension, formally confirmed for the Ruthenian Church at the Synod of Zamość (1720) and preserved in the 1907 Lviv Stauropegion Pentecostarion.

[^2806]: The opening stichera at "Lord, I have cried" in Tone 6 meditate on the institution of the Holy Mystery of the Eucharist at the Mystical Supper (Matthew 26:26-28; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26), calling Christ the "Living Bread" (*Хлѣ́бъ живо́тный*) and "Heavenly Bread" (*Хлѣ́бъ сы́й нбⷭ҇ный*).

[^2807]: The fourth sticheron juxtaposes the earthly manna eaten by the Israelites in the wilderness with the true Bread from Heaven (John 6:49-51, 58), the Angelic Bread (*Хлѣ́бъ А҆́гг҃льскїй*) that imparts everlasting life.

[^2808]: The Doxasticon in Tone 6 summons all lovers of the feasts to rejoice without the "old leaven of malice" (1 Corinthians 5:7-8), partaking of the Lamb of God Who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29).

[^2809]: Physical leaf p621 corresponds to printed folio 615 (`х҃єі`). Conclusion of the Doxasticon at Great Vespers for the Feast of the Most Holy Eucharist (Corpus Christi), followed by the Entrance and the Old Testament Readings (Paroimiai).

[^2810]: The first Old Testament Reading is Exodus 19:10–19, recounting the Lord's descent upon Mount Sinai in fire and smoke to sanctify Israel, prefiguring the awe and moral purification required before partaking of the Holy Mysteries.

[^2811]: The second Old Testament Reading is 1 Kingdoms (1 Samuel) 21:1–6, in which Ahimelech the priest gives the holy Showbread (Bread of Presentation) to David and his companions after ascertaining their ritual purity, prefiguring the Eucharist as the Holy Bread reserved for the faithful.

[^2812]: The third Old Testament Reading is 3 Kingdoms (1 Kings) 17:1–9, wherein ravens miraculously nourish the Prophet Elijah at the brook Cherith with bread and meat, pointing forward to the miraculous food from heaven.

[^2813]: Physical leaf p622 corresponds to printed folio 616 (`х҃ѕі`). Conclusion of the third reading (3 Kingdoms 17:10–16, Elijah and the widow of Zarephath with the unfailing jar of meal and cruse of oil), followed by the Litiya stichera in Tone 6, the Doxasticon in Tone 2, and the opening of the Aposticha in Tone 1.

[^2814]: The first Litiya sticheron in Tone 6 evokes King David leaping and dancing before the Ark of the Covenant (2 Kingdoms / 2 Samuel 6:14–16), contrasting the shadow of the old Ark (which contained the manna and tables of stone) with Christ Himself, the living Lawgiver and incarnate God concealed in the Eucharistic bread.

[^2815]: The second Litiya sticheron recalls the Ark of the Covenant captured by the Philistines and set in the temple of Dagon (1 Kingdoms / 1 Samuel 5:2–4), where the idol fell prostrate and was shattered before the glory of the Lord.

[^2816]: The third and fourth Litiya stichera beseech Christ, the Lamb of God and supernatural Bread, not to consume the communicant as an idol or sinner, but to deify and enlighten through His Body and Blood.

[^2817]: Physical leaf p623 corresponds to printed folio 617 (`х҃зі`). Stichera at the Aposticha (with psalm verses LXX Ps. 77:25 and 77:24), Aposticha Doxasticon in Tone 8, Festal Troparion in Tone 7, Dismissal of Vespers, and the opening of Matins.

[^2818]: The Aposticha Doxasticon in Tone 8 *Ѡ҆ пресла́вное чꙋ́до* ("O marvelous wonder! The Living and Divine Bread...") cites St. Paul's injunction that each examine himself before eating and drinking (1 Corinthians 11:28).

[^2819]: The Festal Troparion in Tone 7 *Хлѣ́бъ преесте́ственный* ("The supernatural Bread, which Angels and Archangels desire to behold with trembling...") is the primary troparion of the Feast of Corpus Christi in the Ruthenian recension.

[^2820]: The Dismissal of Vespers commemorates the institution of the Eucharist at the Mystical Supper ("giving His own Body to eat and His true Blood to drink for our salvation") alongside the twelve holy Apostles.

[^2821]: Physical leaf p624 corresponds to printed folio 618 (`х҃иі`). Sessional Hymn after the 2nd Kathisma in Tone 4, Polyeleos with Megalynarion and Selected Psalm verses, Sessional Hymn after the Polyeleos, and the 1st Antiphon of the Songs of Ascents in Tone 4.

[^2822]: The Sessional Hymn after the 2nd Kathisma is sung to the melodic model *Tone 4, Podoben: "Speedily anticipate" (Ско́рѡ предварѝ)*, quoting Christ's Eucharistic discourse in John 6:54: "Whoso eats My Flesh, and drinks My Blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day."

[^2823]: The Megalynarion for the Feast of the Most Holy Eucharist: *Велича́емъ тѧ̀ Живодв҃че Хрⷭ҇тѐ* ("We magnify Thee, O Christ Giver of life, Who for our sake didst change bread into Thy Body and wine into Thy Blood...").

[^2824]: The Sessional Hymn after the Polyeleos is chanted to the melodic model *Tone 4, Podoben: "The beauty of thy virginity" (Красотѣ̀ дѣ́вства)*, meditating on the transition from the Old Passover to the New Mystical Passover in the Upper Room.

[^2827]: The Post-Gospel Sticheron in Tone 6 *Дне́сь А҆́ггли оу҆жаса́ются* describes the angels filled with awe beholding the incarnate God hidden within the Eucharistic species and received by mortals.

[^2828]: The Canon of the Feast is composed in Tone 2 to the heirmos *Грядѣ́те лю́дїе* ("Come, O ye peoples, let us sing a song unto Christ God, Who divided the sea..."), with the festal refrain: *Сла́ва Хрⷭ҇тѐ Пло́ти твое́й и҆ Кро́ви* ("Glory, O Christ, to Thy Body and Blood!").

[^2831]: Ode 4 begins with the heirmos *Прише́лъ є҆сѝ ѿ Дв҃ы* ("Thou didst come forth from the Virgin, neither an envoy nor an angel..."), based on the Canticle of Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3).

[^2834]: The heirmos of Ode 5 *Просвѣще́нїе во тмѣ̀ лежа́щихъ* ("O illumination of them that lie in darkness...") is based on the Canticle of Isaiah (Isaiah 26:9–20). The second troparion invokes the burning coal of Isaiah 6:6–7 (*оу҆́гль*) to purge the darkened soul.

[^2835]: The heirmos of Ode 6 *Въ бе́зднѣ грѣхо́внѣй валя́ѧся* ("Wallowing in the abyss of sin...") reflects the Canticle of Jonah (Jonah 2).

[^2838]: The Kontakion in Tone 2 *Сѐ предлежи́тъ Хрⷭ҇то́съ на пи́щꙋ всѣ̑мъ* ("Behold, Christ is set forth as food for all...") implores the Lord that the reception of the Mysteries not burn the unworthy, but consume sins and purify souls.

[^2839]: The Synaxarion for Corpus Christi is a major historical and canonical monument of the Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church, detailing how the local Synod of Zamość (1720) formally adopted this solemn feast from the Roman Church to glorify the Holy Eucharist and confirm the faithful in Catholic dogma. Pope Urban IV instituted the universal feast of Corpus Christi in 1264 through the bull *Transiturus de hoc mundo*.

[^2840]: The Synaxarion cites St. John Chrysostom's Eucharistic homilies (on 1 Corinthians 10 and Matthew 26) regarding how Christ feeds believers with His own Body and Blood like a mother nursing her infant, and references the Council of Trent's decrees (Session XIII, Decree on the Eucharist, Canon 6) approving Eucharistic processions (*літі́а* / *processio*) through public squares and streets.

[^2878]: The Stichera at the Aposticha in Tone 2 employ Psalm verses from LXX Ps. 110:4 ("He hath made a remembrance of His wonders") and LXX Ps. 110:9 ("He sent redemption unto His people"), along with LXX Ps. 33:9 ("Taste and see that the Lord is good").

[^2879]: Physical leaf p638 corresponds to printed folio 632 (`х҃лв`). Matins on Saturday (Day 3 of the Octave) with Stichera at the Aposticha in Tone 1, Great Vespers on Saturday Evening, and Sunday Matins rubrics.

[^2880]: The Stichera at the Aposticha on Saturday morning are sung to the melodic model *Tone 1, Podoben: "Joy of the heavenly hosts" (Небе́сныхъ чинѡ́въ)*, meditating on the Upper Room and Christ's words in Luke 22:15–18.

[^2881]: The rubric for Saturday Vespers and Sunday Matins provides the Typikon order for combining the Sunday of the Octave of Corpus Christi with the Resurrectional Octoechos (Tone 6).

[^2882]: Physical leaf p639 corresponds to printed folio 633 (`х҃лг`). Great Vespers on Sunday Evening (Octave Day 4) with Stichera at "Lord, I have cried" in Tone 6, Doxasticon in Tone 3, and Stichera at the Aposticha in Tone 6.

[^2883]: The first Sticheron at "Lord, I have cried" recounts the preparation of the Passover in Matthew 26:17–28 and Luke 22:7–20.

[^2884]: The second Sticheron recalls King David bringing the Ark of the Covenant from the house of Obed-edom to Jerusalem with dancing and instruments (2 Kingdoms / 2 Samuel 6:10–15), identifying the Ark as a prefiguration of the Holy of Holies of the Eucharistic Body and Blood. The Church Slavonic reads *А҆веда́рова* (representing Obed-edom, Hebrew *‘Ōḇēḏ-’Ĕḏōm*).

[^2885]: The Stichera at the Aposticha on Sunday Evening return to the type of Isaac blessing Jacob and Esau (Genesis 27:28–37).

[^2886]: Physical leaf p640 corresponds to printed folio 634 (`х҃лд`). Conclusion of Sunday Evening Aposticha, Doxasticon in Tone 8, and Matins on Monday (Day 5 of the Octave) with Stichera at the Aposticha in Tone 4 and Doxasticon in Tone 2.

[^2887]: The Aposticha Doxasticon in Tone 8 weaves together Christ's invitation in John 7:37–38 ("If any man thirst, let him come unto Me, and drink. He that believs on Me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water") with John 6:56.

[^2888]: The Stichera at the Aposticha at Monday Matins are sung to the melodic model *Tone 4, Podoben: "As one valiant" (Ꙗ҆́кѡ до́блѧ)*.

[^2889]: The Doxasticon in Tone 2 marvels at the Eucharistic presence: how He Whom heaven and earth cannot contain is wholly present in a small host (*въ ма́ницѣ*) and particle of bread, with His Godhead, Flesh, and Divine Soul. The Slavonic *ма́ницѣ* is the locative of *ма́ница* (from Latin *mica* / *manna*, here referring to the consecrated Host / particle).

[^2890]: Feast of the Most Holy Eucharist (Corpus Christi) Octave. The feast of the Most Holy Eucharist was instituted in the Ruthenian Church by the Provincial Council of Zamość (1720), with an eight-day post-festive octave concluding on the following Thursday.

[^2928]: The Provincial Council of Cologne (*Concilium Coloniense*), convoked in 1423 under Archbishop-Elector Dietrich II von Moers, instituted the Feast of the Sorrows/Compassion of Our Lady (*Commemoratio angustiae et doloris B. Mariae V.*) to counter the iconoclastic sacrileges of the Hussites.

[^2929]: Pope Benedict XIV (Prospero Lorenzo Lambertini, 1675–1758; reigned 1740–1758), eminent canonist and liturgical scholar, author of the definitive treatise *De Festis Domini Nostri Jesu Christi et Beatae Mariae Virginis* (1748).

[^2930]: The Hussite iconoclasts in Bohemia and the Rhineland in the early 15th century, who attacked devotion to sacred images, particularly representations of the suffering Mother of God at the Foot of the Cross.

[^2931]: The Provincial Synod of Zamość (*Synodus Provincialis Zamoscena*), convoked in 1720 by Metropolitan Lev Kyshka of Kyiv and the Ruthenian Greek Catholic hierarchy, formally incorporated the Feast of the Compassion of the Theotokos into the liturgical calendar of the Ruthenian Church (Titulus III, *De festis*).

[^2932]: The Tenth Friday after Pascha (*Десята п'ятниця по Пасці*), an ancient popular Ruthenian votive observance dating back to the medieval period, reverenced throughout Galicia, Volhynia, and Belarus. The Synod of Zamość purposefully consecrated this existing folk devotion to the liturgical feast of the Compassion of the Mother of God.

[^2933]: *Hyperphileotheotokos* (Greek: Ὑπερφιλοθεοτόκος, "surpassing in love toward the Mother of God"): A scholarly title used in Western theological and liturgical literature to describe the Greek Patristic tradition's sublime Marian veneration.

[^2935]: Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430), whose sermons on the Passion emphasize the spiritual martyrdom of Mary at the Cross (*passio cordis* / *martyrium spiritus*).

[^2955]: Rubrics governing the occurrence of the Feast of the Annunciation (March 25) upon Lazarus Saturday (*Kyrio-Annunciation* sequence).

[^2956]: Paschal Key K [20]: In the Paschal computer matrix (*Ключъ границъ* / *Clavis Paschalis*), the Slavonic numeral letter K denotes key 20, corresponding to Pascha occurring on April 2, and the Annunciation falling precisely on Lazarus Saturday (March 25).

[^2957]: Galatians 3:27: The baptismal troparion sung at the Divine Liturgy in place of the Trisagion on Lazarus Saturday, Holy Saturday, Bright Week, and Pentecost.

[^2958]: Rubrics governing the coincidence of the Annunciation (March 25) with Palm Sunday (The Entry of the Lord into Jerusalem; Paschal Key Л [21], Pascha on April 1).

[^2959]: Rubrics governing the coincidence of the Annunciation (March 25) with Great and Holy Monday (Paschal Key М [22], Pascha on March 31).

[^2960]: The continuous liturgical reading of the Four Gospels (Tetra-Gospel / *Четвероевангелие*) distributed across the Hours of Great Monday, Great Tuesday, and Great Wednesday.

[^2961]: Psalm 131:13 [132:13]: The canonical Communion Hymn of the Annunciation: "For the Lord hath elected Sion; He hath chosen it for a habitation unto Himself."

[^2962]: Typikon concession and pastoral adaptation for smaller monastic sketes or parish churches where the Divine Liturgy cannot be celebrated on Great Monday.

[^2963]: Rubrics governing the coincidence of the Annunciation (March 25) with Great and Holy Tuesday (Paschal Key Н [23], Pascha on March 30).

[^2964]: Rubrics governing the coincidence of the Annunciation (March 25) with Great and Holy Wednesday (Paschal Key Ѯ [24], Pascha on March 29).

[^2965]: Rubrics governing the coincidence of the Annunciation (March 25) with Great and Holy Thursday (Paschal Key О [25], Pascha on March 28).

[^2966]: Physical Leaf p661 (Printed Folio 325r). The rubric governs the daytime Hours on Great Thursday when the Annunciation of the Mother of God coincides therewith. In Byzantine-Ruthenian practice, the monastic community processes outside the enclosure for the solemn reading of the Hours in the outer narthex, alternating the penitential Triodion Kontakia with the Festal Kontakion of the Annunciation.

[^2967]: The replacement of the Cherubic Hymn and Communion Hymn by the Great Thursday Troparion "Of Thy mystical supper" (*Ве́чери твоеѧ̀ та́йныѧ*) is observed at the evening Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great, even when united with the Annunciation. In temples dedicated to the Annunciation, however, the Heirmos of the 9th Ode of the Feast (*"As unto an animated ark of God"*) replaces the customary Heirmos of Saint Basil (*"The Master's hospitality"*).

[^2968]: In the classical Studite and Ruthenian monastic Typika, the feast of the Annunciation softens the strict fasting rules of Great Week: wine and oil are permitted on Great Thursday evening and on Great Friday, though fish remains forbidden during Great Week.

[^2969]: At the Passion Matins (the Service of the Twelve Gospels) celebrated on Thursday evening / Friday morning, the Festal Gospel of the Annunciation is interpolated into the sequence after the 6th Passion Gospel, accompanied by the Anabathmoi of Tone 4.

[^2970]: On Great Friday, normally a strictly aliturgical day on which no Eucharistic Liturgy may be celebrated, the coincidence of the Annunciation mandates the celebration of the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom following Vespers in the afternoon, an extraordinary exception highlighting the supreme dignity of the Incarnation.

[^2971]: Physical Leaf p661 (Printed Folio 325v). The rubrics for Great Saturday evening begin on Friday afternoon at the 9th hour (3:00 PM), uniting Great Vespers with the five readings of the Annunciation alongside the daily Old Testament prophecies.

[^2972]: Physical Leaf p662 (Printed Folio 326r). The burial office at Great Saturday Matins incorporates the Epitaphios Troparia in Tone 2 (*"The noble Joseph"*, *"When Thou didst descend unto death"*, *"Unto the myrrh-bearing women"*) followed immediately by the Festal Troparion of the Annunciation (*"Today is the fountainhead of our salvation"*).

[^2973]: At the Great Saturday Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great, the 15 Old Testament readings are augmented by the festal readings of the Annunciation, and the baptismal hymn *"As many of you as have been baptized into Christ"* replaces the Trisagion.

[^2974]: The Apodosis (*ѡ҆тда́нїе*) of the Annunciation is suppressed whenever March 25 falls on or after Lazarus Saturday, because the solemnities of Holy Week and Bright Week completely supersede any secondary commemoration. Its hymnography is therefore anticipated at Compline during the Sixth Week of Great Lent.

[^2975]: Physical Leaf p662 (Printed Folio 326v). This ornamental headpiece introduces Part VIII of the 1907 Lviv Pentecostarion: the Typikon Appendix governing Paschaltide Menaion combinations and the Eleven Resurrection Gospel Pillars.

[^2976]: Kyriopascha (*Кѷрїопа́сха*): the rare astronomical and liturgical coincidence wherein the Feast of the Annunciation (March 25) falls on the very Day of Holy Pascha, occurring under Paschal Key 3 (*клю́чь Пасха́лїи Г*). In the Julian calendar, this occurs only in years such as 1817, 1828, 1912, and 2075.

[^2977]: Physical Leaf p663 (Printed Folio 327r). At Paschal Matins on Kyriopascha, the Canons of Pascha and the Annunciation are interwoven on 16 (8 troparia each), with both choirs joining in the center of the temple for the combined Katavasia.

[^2978]: Patristic readings appointed for Paschal Matins include the Paschal Orations of Saint Gregory the Theologian: Oration 45 (*In Sanctum Pascha*, opening with Habakkuk's watch: *"Upon my watch I will stand"*) and Oration 1 (*In Sanctum Pascha*, opening: *"It is the day of Resurrection"*).

[^2979]: Physical Leaf p663 (Printed Folio 327v). At the Liturgy of Kyriopascha, the Paschal Gospel (John 1:1-17) is proclaimed dialogically by the Priest and Deacon, followed by the Annunciation Gospel (Luke 1:24-38) read by a single Deacon without the traditional ringing of the censer bells.

[^2980]: The liturgical order for the Annunciation when falling on Bright Monday, Bright Tuesday, or Bright Wednesday balances the joyous Paschal hymnography with the Annunciation propers.

[^2981]: At Great Vespers on the evening of Pascha (or Bright Monday/Tuesday evening), the Gospel pericopa 65 from Saint John (John 20:19-25) recounting the appearance of the Risen Lord to the disciples in the upper room is solemnly proclaimed from the sanctuary facing the people.

[^2982]: Physical Leaf p664 (Printed Folio 328r). Typikon Chapter governing the Feast of the Holy Great-Martyr George the Trophy-bearer (April 23), whose commemoration can fall anywhere from Great Friday unto Thursday of the Fifth Week after Pascha.

[^2983]: If the Feast of Saint George coincides with Great Friday, Holy Saturday, or Pascha itself, the entire liturgical office of the Saint is transferred to Bright Monday, where it is sung jointly with the Bright Week service.

[^2984]: Physical Leaf p664 (Printed Folio 328v). Rubrics governing the coincidence of Saint George with Thomas Sunday (Antipascha), the Second Sunday of Pascha.

[^2985]: Physical Leaf p665 (Printed Folio 329r). Patristic homily appointed for Thomas Sunday Matins: Saint Gregory the Theologian, Oration 44 (*In novam Dominicam*, opening: *"To be honored by renewals"* / *Ѡ҆бновле́нїємъ чти́тисѧ*).

[^2986]: Physical Leaf p665 (Printed Folio 329v). Rubrics for Saint George when coinciding with the Third Sunday of Pascha (Myrrh-bearing Women), Fourth Sunday (Paralytic), or Fifth Sunday (Samaritan Woman).

[^2987]: Paschal Key 7 (*клю́чь Пасха́лїи З*): calculates the calendar alignment where April 23 (St. George) falls on Wednesday of Mid-Pentecost, and Key (7) where May 8 (St. John the Theologian) coincides with Mid-Pentecost.

[^2988]: Physical Leaf p666 (Printed Folio 330r). At the blessing of the loaves for Saint John the Theologian, the reading is taken from the Book of Revelation (*во А҆покали́ѱїи*), of which he is the inspired author.

[^2989]: Physical Leaf p666 (Printed Folio 330v). Typikon Chapter governing the Feast of the Holy Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian (May 8), which falls between Thomas Saturday and the Friday of the Holy Fathers of the First Ecumenical Council.

[^2990]: Rubrics for Saint John the Theologian when coinciding with Wednesday of the Sixth Week (the Apodosis of Pascha). The midnight office is adapted with Paschal troparia, and the Paschal Canon at Matins is sung without the customary Marian Theotokia.

[^2991]: Physical Leaf p667 (Printed Folio 331r). Coincidence of Saint John the Theologian with the Great Feast of the Ascension of the Lord (Thursday of the Sixth Week). The commemoration of Saint Arsenius the Great (May 8) is transferred.

[^2992]: Physical Leaf p667 (Printed Folio 331v). Coincidence of Saint John the Theologian with the Sunday of the 318 Holy Fathers of the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea (Seventh Sunday of Pascha).

[^2993]: Physical Leaf p668 (Printed Folio 332r). Typikon Chapter governing the Third Finding of the Honorable Head of the Holy Glorious Prophet, Forerunner and Baptist John (May 25), when coinciding with the Sunday of the Holy Fathers.

[^2994]: Physical Leaf p668 (Printed Folio 332v). If the Third Finding of the Forerunner's Head falls on Memorial Saturday of the Departed before Pentecost or on Pentecost Sunday itself, the service is transferred to Thursday of the Seventh Week.

[^2995]: Physical Leaf p669 (Printed Folio 333r). Typikon chapter regulating the combination of the Paschal Pentecostarion (Triodion) with the daily Menaion on weekdays from Thomas Sunday unto the Apodosis of Pentecost.

[^2996]: Detailed rules for combining stichera at Vespers and odes of the canons at Matins based on the rank of the Menaion saint: simple saint (on 3), six-troparion saint (on 6), or Polyeleos saint.

[^2997]: Physical Leaf p670 (Printed Folio 334r). Typikon Chapter governing the Saturday services of the Pentecostarion from Thomas Saturday through the Saturday of the Samaritan Woman.

[^2998]: Temple canon rule: canons dedicated to the titular patron of the local temple are sung on Saturdays of Pentecost if dedicated to a saint, but if the temple is dedicated to the Savior or to the Mother of God, the temple canon is omitted in favor of the Triodion canon of the season.

[^2999]: Physical Leaf p670 (Printed Folio 334v). Rubrics governing the rotation of the Resurrection Troparia (*"The noble Joseph"*, *"When Thou didst descend unto death"*, *"Unto the myrrh-bearing women"*) across the Little Hours (1st, 3rd, 6th, and 9th) during the Week of the Myrrh-bearing Women.

[^3000]: Physical Leaf p671 (Printed Folio 335r). Conclusion of the Saturday Typikon rubrics from leaf p670 for the weeks of the Paralytic, Samaritan Woman, and Blind Man, specifying the alternation of festal and sanctoral Troparia and Kontakia across the Little Hours.

[^3001]: The admonition instructs the monastic Superior (*настоѧ́тель*) and Ekklesiarches (*є҆кклисїа́рхъ*) to exercise pastoral discernment in harmonizing the Pentecostarion (Triodion) with the daily commemorations of the Menaion during the liturgical cycle of the fifty days.

[^3002]: Physical Leaf p671 (Printed Folio 335r). This final canonical rubric of the 1907 Lviv Pentecostarion regulates the correlation between the eleven Matins Resurrection Gospels (*столпѝ Є҆ѵⷢ҇лїй воскре́сныхъ ꙋ҆́тренныхъ*), the eight Tones of the Oktoechos, and the liturgical Epistle and Gospel pericopes read at the Divine Liturgy.

[^3003]: The 11 Sunday Matins Gospels rotate cyclically starting on All Saints Sunday (1st Sunday after Pentecost) with Gospel 1 (Matthew 28:16-20) in Tone 8. Beginning with the 2nd Sunday after Pentecost (Tone 1, Gospel 2), the 8 Tones and 11 Gospels advance in uninterrupted progression throughout the entire liturgical year through Great Lent up to Palm Sunday (*Недѣ́лѧ Цвѣтоно́сїѧ*), regardless of calendar shifts or the date of Pascha. The six pillars (*столпы̀*) represent the six complete 11-week cycles tabulated in the Visual Paschalion (*Зрѧ́чаѧ Пасха́лїѧ*) of the Horologion (*Часосло́въ*).

[^3004]: Because the moveable date of Pascha yields between 32 and 37 weeks between Pentecost and Great Lent, a complete ecclesiastical year typically utilizes between 40 and 45 Sundays from All Saints to Palm Sunday. Thus, while 6 full cycles of 11 Gospels would total 66 Sundays—more than any single liturgical year contains—all six pillars are codified in the tables so that even in the longest possible liturgical year, the sequence never runs short before Palm Sunday.

[^3005]: A critical liturgical distinction between the Divine Liturgy and Matins: The table of "omissions and additions" (*ѡ҆ прїѧ́тїи и҆ ѡ҆ставле́нїи*) in the Liturgikon (*Слꙋже́бникъ / Лїтꙋргі́онъ*) applies strictly to the Liturgy Epistles and Gospels, which terminate their regular post-Pentecost series at the 32nd Sunday after Pentecost (Zacchaeus) or the Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee (*Недѣ́лѧ ѡ҆ Мытарѣ̀ и҆ Фарисе́и*). When the date of Pascha requires adjustments (the "Lucan jump" and supplementary pericopes), only the Liturgy readings are skipped or repeated; the Sunday Oktoechos Tones and Matins Resurrection Gospels proceed without any omission or repetition straight through to Palm Sunday. The physical paper on leaf 335r exhibits historical adhesive repair and surface paper abrasion across lines 6-8 of this rubric, where the restored phrases are placed within brackets.

[^3006]: The master colophon (*Коне́цъ, и҆ Бг҃ꙋ сла́ва* — "The End, and to God be glory") formally concludes the printing of the monumental 1907 Lviv Stauropegion Paschal Pentecostarion (*Трїѡ́дь Цвѣтна́ѧ*), published under the blessing and episcopal approbation of Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky and the Stauropegion Institute in Lviv.
